generate.help.prompt.title: Prompt
generate.help.prompt.body: A plain description of what you want to see: the subject first, then where it is and how it looks. Concrete nouns and adjectives have the most effect, and anything you do not describe is still decided, using whatever was most common in the model's training images.
generate.help.negative.title: Negative prompt
generate.help.negative.body: A second prompt naming what you do not want to see. It pushes the image away from those words and is not a quality switch, so it works best as a short list of things you do not want in the picture.
generate.help.prompt_emphasis.title: Word emphasis
generate.help.prompt_emphasis.body: Writing part of a prompt as (a phrase:1.2) changes how much weight that phrase has. Values close to 1 change little; above about 1.5 the phrase starts to distort the rest of the picture.
generate.help.size.title: Width & height
generate.help.size.body: The size the image is drawn at, not a crop of something larger, so changing it changes the picture. The size presets set both values at once, and a larger image costs more time and kudos.
generate.help.native_resolution.title: Native resolution
generate.help.native_resolution.body: Every model was trained at a size: around 512 a side for Stable Diffusion 1.5 and 1024 for SDXL. Ask for much less and you get a worse picture rather than a smaller one, with the subject cramped or gone.
generate.help.oversize.title: Going past native size
generate.help.oversize.body: Ask a model for much more than its native size and it repeats what it knows instead of filling the space, so you get a second head or an extra arm. Hires fix is the way around it.
generate.help.steps.title: Steps
generate.help.steps.body: How many denoising passes the model makes. More steps can add detail but cost more time and kudos, and most models stop improving somewhere between 20 and 40.
generate.help.cfg.title: Guidance (CFG)
generate.help.cfg.body: How strictly the model follows your prompt. Low values drift away from it; high values give hard edges and oversaturated colour. 5 to 10 suits most models, and distilled models such as Flux Schnell want 1 or 2.
generate.help.sampler.title: Sampler
generate.help.sampler.body: The method that turns noise into an image. Samplers differ in speed and character more than in quality; k_euler and k_dpmpp_2m are safe starting points. The Recommended and Advanced groups are a suggestion and nothing more; every sampler is accepted. A few samplers run the model two or three times per step; the note under the list says so, and the kudos estimate includes it.
generate.help.scheduler.title: Schedule
generate.help.scheduler.body: How the noise levels are spaced across the steps. Karras and normal suit most models; the others are spacings for particular models or very low step counts. Which schedules are offered depends on the sampler and the model family, so the list changes when those change.
generate.help.sampler_settings.title: Sampler settings
generate.help.sampler_settings.body: Extra controls that some samplers offer, such as how much fresh noise they add back at each step, or which internal method they use. Only the ones the sampler accepts are shown, and leaving them blank keeps the worker's own defaults, which is what nearly every image is made with.
generate.help.flow_shift.title: Flow shift
generate.help.flow_shift.body: Shifts where a flow-matching model spends its steps: higher values give more of them to the coarse structure, lower values to fine detail. Only Flux and Qwen Image models read it, so the field only appears when one is selected.
generate.help.karras.title: Karras sigmas
generate.help.karras.body: Spaces the sampler's noise levels using the Karras schedule. It often sharpens results at low step counts, and some models are trained expecting it while others are not.
generate.help.hires.title: Hires fix
generate.help.hires.body: Renders at the model's native size first, then upscales and refines that image. It is the usual cure for the duplicated limbs and repeated subjects you get when a small model is asked for a large image. The size presets change to match when hires fix is on, since drawing above the native size is the point of it.
generate.help.tiling.title: Tiling
generate.help.tiling.body: Makes the edges of the image wrap, so copies of it laid side by side join without a seam. Worth turning on for backgrounds, fabrics and ground textures, and of no use for a picture you are only going to look at once. The examples show one render repeated nine times and the same render as a single tile, because a seam only exists where one copy meets the next.
generate.help.hires_denoise.title: Hires denoise
generate.help.hires_denoise.body: How much the second pass may repaint the upscaled image. Lower keeps the first pass's composition, higher lets the model add detail and drift from it.
generate.help.denoise.title: Denoising strength
generate.help.denoise.body: How much of your picture the model repaints. Low values stay close to it, and near 1 almost nothing of it survives. With a control type set, the worker starts from a blank canvas and your picture is only read by the detector, so leave denoise at 1 unless you know why you want less. Control strength is what says how closely the image follows the control map. On older versions of the horde, denoise did that job.
generate.help.control_type.title: Control type
generate.help.control_type.body: The control type says which map of your picture the image follows. An outline detector keeps the shapes and lets the colours change. A depth detector keeps the arrangement in space and lets the drawing change. Pick the one that reads the part you want kept. Nine control types are served by any worker that offers ControlNet. The rest need a recently updated worker, so those requests reach fewer workers and can wait longer.
generate.help.control_strength.title: Control strength
generate.help.control_strength.body: Control strength says how closely the image follows the control map. Leave it unset and the request carries nothing for it, so the worker uses its own 1, and at 1 the image already follows the map closely. Below 0.25 the map barely matters. 0.5 to 0.9 is the range worth trying. Above about 1.75 the colours start to wash out. The horde takes 0.01 to 3, and only with a control type set or the QR code workflow on; a request that carries a strength with neither is refused. Only workers that were updated recently are handed a request that sets it.
generate.help.control_map.title: Control map
generate.help.control_map.body: A control map is the drawing a detector makes from your picture: the outlines it finds, how far away each part is, or where the joints of a body are. The image follows that drawing rather than your picture. The worker normally draws the map for you, so there is nothing to set here.
generate.help.clip_skip.title: CLIP skip
generate.help.clip_skip.body: Stops reading your prompt this many layers before the end of the text encoder. 1 is standard; many anime-derived models are trained for 2.
generate.help.seed.title: Seed
generate.help.seed.body: The number the image's starting noise is generated from. The same seed with the same settings reproduces the same image. Leave it blank for a fresh random one each time, and only set one once you have a picture you like and want to change one thing about.
generate.help.model.title: Model
generate.help.model.body: The trained network that draws the picture. Each model was taught on a different set of images, so each has its own look, its own strengths and its own native size; the list is whatever the workers online are carrying, so it changes without you touching it. Leave it blank and the horde picks any available model.
generate.help.post.title: Post-processing
generate.help.post.body: Passes run over the finished image after generation: Upscale to enlarge it, Face fix to redraw small faces, or Remove background to cut the subject out. None of them changes the composition, and each costs a little extra time and kudos.
generate.help.step_preview.title: Steps of one render
generate.help.step_preview.body: One picture, captured after each denoising pass. The pictures run in order from the first pass to the last: random noise at the beginning, the finished picture at the end. The model's guess shown with each one is what the model expected the finished picture to be at that point.
generate.help.tis.title: Embeddings
generate.help.tis.body: An embedding teaches the model one new word. You then use that word in your prompt, and it does nothing until the word appears there, so either add it yourself or let the horde put it in the prompt or the negative prompt for you.
generate.help.loras.title: LoRAs & embeddings
generate.help.loras.body: LoRAs are small add-on files that bias a model towards a particular subject or style, and embeddings do the same through one word added to the prompt. Strength sets how much each one changes the result. A generation carries at most five LoRAs and twenty embeddings, and a worker has to be able to download a file before it can serve your request.
generate.help.upscaler.title: Upscale
generate.help.upscaler.body: Enlarges the finished image with an upscaling model. It runs after generation, so it costs extra time and kudos but does not change the composition.
generate.help.facefixer.title: Face fix
generate.help.facefixer.body: Runs a face restoration model over the result. GFPGAN and CodeFormers repair small or distorted faces, at the cost of a little extra time.
generate.help.facefixer_strength.title: Face fix strength
generate.help.facefixer_strength.body: How strongly the face fixer is applied. It is only sent when a face fixer is selected, and high values clean up more but can make every face look alike.
generate.help.strip_background.title: Remove background
generate.help.strip_background.body: Hands the finished image to a background remover, which cuts the subject out and leaves the rest transparent. It runs after generation, so the picture itself is already decided. Hair and other fine edges are where the cut shows.
generate.help.batch.title: Batch count
generate.help.batch.body: How many images this request asks for. Each one is charged its own kudos and shares your settings apart from the seed.
generate.help.transparent.title: Transparent background
generate.help.transparent.body: Asks for an image with a transparent background rather than a painted one. Only Stable Diffusion 1.5 and SDXL models use this and the worker has to support it. It is not the same as the Remove background post-processor, which cuts the subject out afterwards.
generate.help.qr.title: QR code
generate.help.qr.body: Draws a scannable QR code carrying this text or URL into the image. It needs a Stable Diffusion 1.5 or SDXL model, and these requests are never batched, so each image is queued on its own.
generate.help.webhook.title: Webhook URL
generate.help.webhook.body: An http(s) address the horde POSTs each finished generation to, for automation. Leave it blank if you are only using this page; an address that is not a valid URL is left off the request rather than failing it.
generate.help.workers.title: Worker targeting
generate.help.workers.body: Names the workers that may take this request. With Only these workers, only the workers you list can take the request. With Avoid these workers, any worker except those can take it. Type a worker ID, or press Pick from the workers online to choose from the list, which also shows which of them carry your model. With Only these workers, a note under the list says when a listed worker cannot serve the request as set. The list holds at most five workers, and a short list usually means a longer wait.
generate.help.remember_extras.title: Remembering extras
generate.help.remember_extras.body: Keeps the webhook URL and worker list in this browser between visits. Turn it off if you would rather they reset when you reload.
generate.help.trusted_workers.title: Trusted workers
generate.help.trusted_workers.body: Restricts the request to workers the horde has marked as trusted. Far fewer workers qualify, so expect a longer wait in exchange for the tighter guarantee.
generate.help.slow_workers.title: Slow workers
generate.help.slow_workers.body: Lets slower workers pick the request up. Leaving it on usually gets you an image sooner; turning it off costs more kudos and favours faster hardware.
generate.help.extra_slow_workers.title: Extra slow workers
generate.help.extra_slow_workers.body: Also allows the slowest workers on the network. It can rescue an unpopular model that nothing else is running, at the cost of a long generation.
generate.help.allow_downgrade.title: Allow downgrade
generate.help.allow_downgrade.body: If you cannot afford the full kudos cost, the horde reduces the request instead of refusing it, usually by cutting the step count.
generate.help.replacement_filter.title: Filter suspicious prompts
generate.help.replacement_filter.body: Lets the horde replace words its filters flag rather than reject the request. Turning it off means a flagged prompt fails outright instead.
generate.help.nsfw.title: NSFW
generate.help.nsfw.body: Marks the request as possibly not safe for work, so only workers that accept NSFW jobs pick it up. Leaving it off for an NSFW prompt risks the job being rejected.
generate.help.censor_nsfw.title: Censor NSFW
generate.help.censor_nsfw.body: This only has an effect while Allow NSFW is off. In that case, if the worker's NSFW check flags the finished image, you get a censored placeholder instead of it. With Allow NSFW on, nothing is censored.
generate.help.source.title: Source image mode
generate.help.source.body: How an attached image is used: img2img repaints it, ControlNet copies its layout (edges, depth, pose) into the new picture, Inpainting repaints only what you mask, and Remix blends it with other images and needs Stable Cascade as your model.
generate.help.img2img.title: img2img
generate.help.img2img.body: The render starts from the picture you attached instead of from noise. Denoising strength decides how much of it survives.
generate.help.img2img_mask.title: Painting a mask
generate.help.img2img_mask.body: Only the part you paint is redrawn, and the picture under the mask is kept as the starting point. Inpainting is different: it clears the masked area first and the model paints new content there. Because the original is still there, Denoising strength works inside the mask exactly as it does without one. Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2 and XL models only.
generate.help.inpainting.title: Inpainting
generate.help.inpainting.body: The masked area is cleared before the model starts, so it invents what belongs there from the prompt and the surroundings. There is no strength to set: below the maximum the area comes back unfinished, which is why the slider is not offered.
generate.help.outpainting.title: Extending the canvas
generate.help.outpainting.body: Outpainting is when your picture is placed inside a larger frame and the model paints the space around it. It is a form of inpainting, where all of the new area is painted instead of only the masked area, so the same rules apply. Set a larger width or height to make room.
generate.help.remix.title: Remix
generate.help.remix.body: Blends your picture with several others, each with its own strength. Stable Cascade models only.
generate.help.requirements.title: Model suggestions
generate.help.requirements.body: Lines marked “Suggested” come from the selected model's own reference entry. They are recommendations, and nothing is enforced: a value the model was not tuned for is flagged, and the request is still sent as you set it.
generate.reference.head: Settings reference
generate.reference.lead: Every setting the control panel has, in the order the panel shows them. Each one says what it is in a sentence, then goes as deep as you want to read. In the panel itself they wait folded, each card showing what it is currently set to; when an image is close but not right, change one thing at a time and hold the seed so you can see what the change did.
generate.reference.link_control_types: See what each control type keeps
generate.reference.link_control_strength: How hard the control map holds
generate.reference.link_alchemy_cut_out: Cutting out a background in alchemy
generate.reference.link_alchemy_control_: Extracting a control map in alchemy
generate.reference.crop_head_strip: One setting against another, close up
generate.reference.crop_head_alchemy: The same picture before and after, close up
generate.reference.crop_note: The same patch cut from both pictures, drawn one picture pixel to one screen pixel.
generate.reference.crop_door_note: Opens the whole picture at this size, on this patch.
generate.reference.section_hint.prompt: What you are asking for, and what you would rather not have.
generate.reference.section_hint.model: Which model paints it, plus the LoRAs laid over the top and the styles: a style is a saved bundle of wording, settings and a model you can browse.
generate.reference.section_hint.size: How large the picture is, and which way round.
generate.reference.section_hint.source: An image you attach, and how the model is allowed to use it.
generate.reference.section_hint.sampling: How the picture is made: steps, guidance, sampler and seed.
generate.reference.section_hint.finishin: What is done to the image once it has been generated.
generate.reference.section_hint.horde: Which workers may take the job, and how the request is handled.
generate.reference.section_hint.workflow: The outputs that are not simply a picture: transparency and QR codes.
generate.reference.quality_negative: Steers away from what you name; it is not a quality switch
generate.reference.quality_prompt_emphas: Past about 1.5 the weighted phrase starts taking the picture apart
generate.reference.quality_size: The shape changes the composition; area past native adds no detail
generate.reference.quality_oversize: One pass past native repeats the subject across the frame
generate.reference.quality_steps: Past the point a model settles, more is not better
generate.reference.quality_cfg: Too low and the picture drifts from your prompt; too high and colours go harsh
generate.reference.quality_sampler: Sets the character of the image; quality is decided elsewhere
generate.reference.quality_scheduler: Mostly visible at low step counts
generate.reference.quality_karras: Often sharper at low step counts
generate.reference.quality_hires_fix: Cures duplicated subjects at large sizes
generate.reference.quality_upscaler: Makes the same picture larger; the composition is already decided
generate.reference.quality_facefixer: Repairs small faces, but makes them look more generic
generate.reference.quality_strip_backgro: Cuts the subject out; fine edges like hair are where it shows
generate.reference.prompt.lead: What you want to see, written as a plain description.
generate.reference.negative.lead: A second prompt naming what you do not want in the picture.
generate.reference.negative.body:
The negative prompt is given to the model on the same passes as the prompt, in the opposite direction. It biases the picture away from those words while the picture is being made. It does not check or filter the finished image.

Two things it does well:

- Naming the failure you keep getting. Anatomy is what usually goes wrong, and hands most of all, which is what the first set of examples shows.
- Removing something you asked for by implication. If your prompt says “skyharbor” you tend to get airships as well, because the two usually appear together. Put “airships” in the negative prompt and they go, and the harbour stays. That is the second set of examples.

It does not work as a quality setting. A copied list like “bad, ugly, worst quality” names nothing in particular, so there is nothing for it to bias the picture away from.

Keep it short and specific, and add to it when you can point at what you are removing. Guidance scales the gap between the two prompts, so the same negative has more effect at 10 than at 3.
generate.reference.prompt_emphasis.lead: Weights that change how much effect one part of your prompt has.
generate.reference.prompt_emphasis.body:
Write a phrase as (a phrase:1.2) and it is weighted by that number.

1 has the same effect as writing the phrase with no parentheses. Below 1 reduces its effect; above 1 increases it. A small change, 1.1 or 1.2, is usually enough for a style word.

The first set of examples walks one style phrase from 0.5 to 2 and shows where the useful range ends. By 1.5 the style dominates and the shapes start to break down. At 2 the picture is no longer usable.

The second set shows what a single gradient cannot. Two phrases are held in one prompt, winter and summer, and traded against each other across the range. Neither is ever removed, and the picture falls wherever the ratio puts it.

A weight sets the balance between the parts of your prompt. Raising one weight lowers the effect of everything else, even though you did not change those numbers.

Reach for it when one part of a prompt is being ignored or is dominating. Reach for plainer wording first when the whole thing is being read loosely.
generate.reference.size.lead: How large the picture is drawn, and which way round.
generate.reference.size.body:
Width and height set the size the picture is drawn at. Changing them gives you a different picture. They do not crop or reframe a picture you already have. Each side moves in steps of 64, between 64 and 3072.

The preset chips set the pair at once and are cut for the selected model's family, which is why the same “portrait 2:3” chip reads 512×768 on a Stable Diffusion 1.5 model and 832×1216 on an SDXL one.

The shape matters as much as the area. A tall frame suits a standing figure and a wide one suits a landscape, and one prompt will compose itself differently in each.

Cost follows area. The horde charges by megapixelsteps, which is the number of pixels multiplied by the number of steps, so doubling both sides costs four times as many kudos.

Which sizes a given model is any good at is a separate question, answered under [[set:native_resolution]].
generate.reference.native_resolution.lea: The size a model was trained at, which is the size it knows a whole scene at.
generate.reference.native_resolution.bod:
Training happened at a fixed size, and a model's competence is built around it: around 512 a side for Stable Diffusion 1.5 and its descendants, and 1024 for SDXL.

Read it as the scale at which the model knows what a whole scene looks like. It is neither a minimum nor a recommendation.

The examples walk one SDXL request down from its native 1024, and each size gives a different picture:

- at 512, bodies are still drawn correctly, but the framing tightens into a close-up of whatever fits;
- at 256 you get a background with no recognisable subject in it;
- at 128 the image is unreadable.

Going the other way breaks differently, by repetition, which is what [[set:oversize]] covers.

The panel knows both native squares and says so. It snaps an untouched size across when you switch to a model of the other family, and it notes when your dimensions have drifted out of the one you are on.

A moderate change is fine, and every aspect preset is a moderate change. Halving or doubling a side is where the picture breaks down.
generate.reference.oversize.lead: What goes wrong when you ask for a picture much larger than the model's native size.
generate.reference.oversize.body:
Past the size it was trained at, the model has no sense of what a whole body or a whole composition looks like at that scale. It repeats what it does know instead, so you get a second head or an extra arm, and skylines that repeat themselves across the frame.

That is why a picture that is wrong at 1536 is often exactly right at 1024. Stable Diffusion 1.5 models start showing it past about 768 on a side, and the panel says so on the size control. SDXL holds on further and then breaks the same way.

There are two ways out, and they are different tools:

- The hires pass generates at a size the model is competent at, then enlarges that image and repaints it, so the composition is decided where it can be decided well.
- An upscaler runs afterwards on the finished picture, which makes it bigger without making it different.

Use one of these whenever you want a picture larger than the model's native size.
generate.reference.tis.lead: A textual inversion, or embedding, teaches a model one new word that you then use in your prompt.
generate.reference.tis.body:
An embedding adds a single token to the prompt vocabulary, and the model paints what that token means. It does nothing until its token actually appears in your prompt. A LoRA is loaded alongside the checkpoint and affects every picture it makes; an embedding waits for its word.

You can ask the horde to add the token for you and say which half of the prompt it belongs in. Put it in the negative prompt for the many embeddings that exist to describe what you do not want. Leave that unset and you type the token yourself.

Strength scales how much effect the token has, and only applies when the horde is inserting it for you.

A generation carries at most twenty embeddings.

An embedding is named by its model page, never by a published version: unlike a LoRA, the horde has no way to be told which version of an embedding you meant.
generate.reference.loras.lead: LoRAs and textual inversions are small add-on files that bias a model towards a character, a style or a concept.
generate.reference.loras.body:
A LoRA is loaded alongside the checkpoint and changes what it paints; a textual inversion does the same through a token you put in the prompt.

Each carries a strength. For a LoRA, the model and CLIP strengths set how much effect it has on the picture and on the reading of the prompt. Around 1 is the usual starting point, and pushing far past it tends to flatten everything else the model knows.

A LoRA is trained for one family of models. One built for Stable Diffusion 1.5 will do little or nothing on an SDXL model. The horde accepts the request either way and gives no error, so the only symptom is a picture the LoRA had no effect on. The picker starts from the family your model belongs to and says so when a selection does not match.

When you add one, a specific published version is pinned, and not whichever is newest at the time. That keeps a saved request meaning the same thing after the author publishes an update. A version is always named by number, which is why typing one by hand asks you to confirm it is a version.

Many LoRAs are trained against a trigger word and do very little without it. You can ask the horde to insert one for you, or add it to your prompt yourself. Triggers longer than thirty characters cannot be sent for insertion, so those are offered as something to add to the prompt instead.

A generation carries at most five LoRAs and twenty embeddings. You can keep more than that selected; the ones past the limit are not sent, and moving one up the list includes it instead.

A worker has to be able to fetch the file before it can serve your request, so an early-access or paid version cannot be used at all, and an obscure add-on can leave the job waiting.
generate.reference.source.lead: Attach a picture and the model starts from it instead of from nothing. There are four ways it can be used, and they are not variations on one idea.
generate.reference.source.body:
Each one has its own page, because each answers a different question:

- [[set:img2img]] redraws the whole picture, keeping as much of it as you allow.
- [[set:img2img_mask]] redraws only where you paint, and keeps what was under the brush as its starting point.
- [[set:inpainting]] also redraws only where you paint, but throws away what was there first.
- [[set:outpainting]] grows the picture outwards and fills in the new space.
- [[set:remix]] blends your picture with several others, and only Stable Cascade models serve it.

ControlNet also reads an attached picture, and it has a page of its own because it never redraws your picture. A detector reads the structure out of it (an outline, a depth map, a pose), and the model paints a new picture that follows that structure.

Masked work of any kind needs a Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2 or XL model. On newer model families the mask is ignored and the whole picture is redrawn. The panel warns you before you spend kudos on it.
generate.reference.img2img.lead: Redraw a picture you already have, keeping as much or as little of it as you choose.
generate.reference.img2img.body:
Your picture is the starting point the model paints over, and [[set:denoise]] decides how much of it may change.

Low, and you get your own picture with a light pass over it: sharper, tidier, the same scene. High, and only the arrangement survives. At 1 your picture is ignored completely, and the result is the same as a plain text-to-image request.

The useful band is the middle, where you can change the weather, the hour or the style and still recognise what you started with.

The size follows the picture. A request whose width and height do not match what you attached will have it stretched to fit.

To change only part of the picture, paint a mask instead of lowering the strength. A lower strength applies everywhere at once. Painting a mask is [[set:img2img_mask]].
generate.reference.img2img_mask.lead: Redraw only the part you paint over, starting from what is already underneath it.
generate.reference.img2img_mask.body:
Turn on “Paint a mask” in image-to-image and the brush appears. Everything you do not paint comes back untouched, pixel for pixel.

What makes this different from [[set:inpainting]] is what happens under the brush. Here the original is kept as the starting point, so [[set:denoise]] means the same thing inside the mask as it does anywhere else: a light pass at low values, a full replacement near 1. Inpainting erases the masked area before it begins, and has nothing to keep.

So the choice between them is really a question about intent. Restyling a coat that should still be that coat is this mode. Replacing it with something else is inpainting.

The examples show the two side by side on one picture and one mask. In the masked image-to-image set, the strength changes the result as you would expect. In the inpainting set it changes almost nothing.

Two things to know before you spend on it. It needs a Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2 or XL model. And it cannot be combined with [[set:hires]]: with a mask attached the enlarging pass never runs and the picture comes back at the smaller size it was drawn at.
generate.reference.inpainting.lead: Replace the part you paint over with something new, and leave the rest alone.
generate.reference.inpainting.body:
The area you mask is cleared away before the model starts. The model is then asked what belongs there, given the prompt and everything around the hole.

That clearing is the whole difference from [[set:img2img_mask]], and it has one consequence worth knowing in advance: there is no strength slider here. The panel sends the maximum and does not offer you the slider. A lower value does not soften the edit; it leaves the area unfinished. The examples show it: at a middling strength the masked area comes back as a flat grey patch in the shape of the brush, because there was nothing left to work from and not enough of the pass left to invent anything.

Use it when what is there should go. Use the masked kind of image-to-image when what is there should change.

Fewer workers serve this than serve an ordinary request, so expect to wait a little longer. It also needs a Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2 or XL model, and it cannot be combined with [[set:hires]].

To make the picture larger by painting new ground around it, see [[set:outpainting]].
generate.reference.outpainting.lead: Grow the picture outwards and let the model fill in what was never there.
generate.reference.outpainting.body:
Turn on “Extend the canvas” in inpainting, set a [[set:size]] larger than the picture you attached, and say where your picture should sit in the new frame. The panel puts it there and asks the model to paint everything around it.

Underneath it is the same job as inpainting, with the empty border standing in for the brush, which is why it behaves the same way: the new ground is blank, so there is no strength to set and the whole area is invented.

What you are really choosing is how much to invent. The examples push one picture out by a narrow border, by half its width again, and finally to twice its original size. The first two carry the scene straight out. The largest one no longer reads as an extension of the original: the model invents a new scene around it. That may be what you want, and it is a different result.

Small steps work better than large ones. If you want a lot more canvas, go out in two or three passes, feeding each result back in. Asking for all of it at once works less well.

Look along the join. The part you attached comes back exactly as it went in, so a seam can show where the two meet, especially at the larger extents.

The same limits as inpainting apply: a Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2 or XL model, fewer workers than usual, and no [[set:hires]].
generate.reference.remix.lead: Blend your picture with several others and let the model find something between them.
generate.reference.remix.body:
Attach a picture, add up to a handful more, and give each of the extras a strength saying how much it should contribute.

There is no [[set:denoise]] here. The blend is the whole control, and it is set per picture rather than once for the request.

Only Stable Cascade models serve it. The panel greys the option out until you pick one, and says why.
generate.reference.denoise.lead: How much of your source image the model is allowed to repaint.
generate.reference.denoise.body:
At low values the result is your picture with a light pass over it; near 1 almost nothing of the original survives.

The middle is where img2img is most useful: enough freedom to change the style or the light, and not so much that the subject moves.

It applies to img2img and inpainting. Remix weights its inputs per image instead, and ignores this.

With a control type set, the worker starts from a blank canvas and your picture is only read by the detector, so there is nothing here for denoise to keep. Leave it at 1 unless you know why you want less. [[set:control_strength]] is what says how closely the image follows the control map. On older versions of the horde, denoise did that job.

It belongs to requests that start from an image. On a plain text prompt leave it at 1, because a lower value quietly cuts steps off the end of the schedule, and a model designed for very few steps, such as Flux Schnell, comes back pale and still speckled with noise.

The examples come in two sets, one on a sampler that re-rolls and one on a sampler that settles. A sampler that re-rolls adds fresh noise back at every pass, so some of what moves across those examples is the sampler and not the strength. The set on the sampler that settles shows the strength on its own.
generate.reference.control_type.lead: Which map of your picture the image follows.
generate.reference.control_type.body:
The image you get back is not a copy of your picture. A detector reads your picture first and draws a control map from it: outlines, a clean line drawing, how far away each part is, which way each surface faces, where the joints of a body are, flat colour fields, or the picture itself. The image the worker makes then follows that map.

So choosing a control type is choosing what has to survive from your picture. Outlines keep the shapes and let the colours, the materials and the style go. Depth keeps the arrangement in space and lets the drawing go. Pose keeps the people and nothing else.

The horde serves ControlNet on Stable Diffusion 1.5 models. Nine control types are served by any worker that offers ControlNet at all. The rest need a recently updated worker, so those requests reach fewer workers and can wait longer.

How closely the image follows the map is a separate setting, the control strength, and its useful range is narrower than it looks: too low and the map is only a suggestion, too high and the image traces it.
generate.reference.control_strength.lead: How closely the image follows the control map a detector drew from your picture.
generate.reference.control_strength.body:
A detector draws a control map from your picture, and control strength says how closely the image follows that map. Leave it unset on your first try. The request then carries nothing for it, and the worker uses its own value of 1, which already follows the map closely. When you want a looser hold, 0.5 to 0.9 is the range worth trying.

Below 0.25 the map barely matters: the image is close to what the prompt alone would give. Between 0.25 and 0.5 you can see the map guiding the image, and most detectors change little above 0.5. The sparse maps, binary and scribble, need up to 0.75. The mlsd (straight lines), openpose and shuffle detectors keep changing the picture at every value, because their maps describe only part of it. The tile and recolor detectors stop changing anything above about 1. Above about 1.75 the colours start to look washed out. The example pictures here were made on local software, one set per detector.

The field takes 0.01 to 3, and only with a control type set or with the QR code workflow, which applies a control map of its own. A request that carries a strength with neither is refused. Only workers that were updated recently are handed a request that sets it, so setting one narrows the group of workers that can take the job.
generate.reference.control_map.lead: Where the control map comes from, and how to get it back on its own.
generate.reference.control_map.body:
The image you get back does not follow your picture directly. A detector reads your picture and draws a control map from it: the outlines it finds, how far away each part is, where the joints of a body are. The image the worker makes follows that drawing.

Normally you hand in an ordinary picture and the worker runs the detector for you, so there is nothing to set here.

Two things change that. If the picture you hand in is already a control map, drawn in alchemy or anywhere else, turn on Image is already a control map and the worker uses it as it stands instead of reading it a second time. If what you want is the drawing rather than an image made from it, turn on Return only the control map, no image and the map comes back on its own.

Which detector runs is the control type, and how closely the image follows the map is the control strength.
generate.reference.steps.lead: How many denoising passes the model makes on its way from noise to a picture.
generate.reference.steps.body:
Each pass refines what the last one left, so more steps can mean more detail, and each one costs time and kudos.

Most models stop improving somewhere between 20 and 40. Past that you are usually paying for a picture nobody can tell from the cheaper one.

How fast a model gets there depends on the sampler as much as on the model: some samplers settle towards a single image, and some re-roll the detail at every count.

Where a model's reference entry suggests a range, the panel marks it on the steps control.
generate.reference.cfg.lead: How strictly the model is pushed to follow your prompt.
generate.reference.cfg.body: Low values let it wander off the prompt and invent; high values force every word in and harden the picture, with sharp edges and burnt colour. Between 5 and 10 suits most models. Distilled models are the exception, and Flux Schnell and its relatives want 1 or 2. Guidance and steps read against each other, so a value that works at 30 steps may not at 10.
generate.reference.sampler.lead: The algorithm that turns the starting noise into an image.
generate.reference.sampler.body:
Samplers differ in character and in how quickly they settle on a picture. There is no best one, and k_euler and k_dpmpp_2m are safe starting points.

What matters for the rest of the panel is how your sampler answers [[set:steps]], and samplers fall into two groups.

A sampler that settles walks steadily towards one image. Raise the steps and you refine the picture you were already getting, and the gain tails off once the picture stops changing.

A sampler that re-rolls adds a small amount of fresh noise back at every pass. Raise the steps and you get a different picture. The extra passes do not make the same picture cleaner, so a step count that suited a sampler that settles may look unfinished here.

Both behaviours are correct, and the difference decides whether it is worth paying for more steps. The names tell you which you have: an _a suffix marks an ancestral sampler and sde marks a stochastic one, and both re-roll.

- The samplers that re-roll are k_euler_a, k_dpm_2_a, k_dpmpp_2s_a and k_dpmpp_sde.
- The samplers that settle are k_euler, k_dpm_2, k_dpmpp_2m, k_heun, k_lms, DDIM, dpmsolver and lcm.

Some models name the samplers they were tuned for, and the panel marks those as suggested.
generate.reference.seed.lead: The number the image's starting noise is generated from.
generate.reference.seed.body:
The same seed with the same settings and the same model gives the same image every time, which is what makes it possible to change one setting and see only that change.

Leave it blank and the horde picks a fresh random seed for each request. That is the normal way to work: you fix the seed once you have a picture you like and want to change one thing about it.

Each image in a batch shares your settings apart from the seed, so a batch is variations rather than copies.
generate.reference.clip_skip.lead: Stops reading your prompt this many layers before the end of the text encoder.
generate.reference.clip_skip.body: The encoder builds meaning up in layers, and stopping early hands the model a looser, less literal reading of what you asked for. 1 is standard and is what most models were trained against. Many anime-derived checkpoints were trained at 2, and on those the difference is not subtle. Where a model states a value, the panel marks it on the CLIP skip control as a suggestion.
generate.reference.scheduler.lead: Which noise schedule the sampler walks: where its stops sit between noise and picture.
generate.reference.scheduler.body:
Steps decide how many stops there are between noise and picture; the schedule decides where those stops sit.

Karras and normal are the two the horde has always offered, and Karras is the default. The rest are newer spacings:

- simple, exponential and beta are general purpose;
- some are cut for very low step counts;
- align_your_steps and gits read the model itself to place their stops, so they are offered only for the model families they were derived for.

The panel asks the horde which schedules the chosen sampler and model accept and offers only those, so a schedule that would be refused never appears. On a horde that publishes no such list, only Karras and normal are offered.

A schedule marked as suggested is one the sampler's own authors pair it with.
generate.reference.sampler_settings.lead: The fine controls a sampler exposes: how much fresh noise it adds back, when, and which internal solver it runs.
generate.reference.sampler_settings.body:
Most samplers take no settings beyond steps and schedule. The ones that do expose these:

- eta and noise scale, on the samplers that add noise back as they go: the ancestral and SDE families. eta decides whether and how much of that noise comes back, and noise scale multiplies it.
- churn, on Euler and Heun. It is a controlled amount of noise stirred in across a window of the run, set by the two churn bounds.
- the solver order, on multistep solvers such as DEIS and IPNDM. A few of those also offer a choice of internal correction: midpoint or Heun, phi_1 or phi_2.

Every field is optional. Left blank, the worker uses the sampler's own default, and every other render in this library was made that way.

The examples move one setting at a time with the rest left at their defaults. The useful room around each default is narrow: a little either way is a visible edit, and a lot of it is grain or a flat picture.
generate.reference.flow_shift.lead: Moves where a flow-matching model spends its steps, between coarse structure and fine detail.
generate.reference.flow_shift.body:
Flux and Qwen Image models do not denoise the way Stable Diffusion does. They follow a path from noise to image, and the shift decides how much of that path is spent on the early, structural part.

Raise it and the composition settles harder while detail gets less attention; lower it and the opposite happens.

Around 2 to 4 suits most prompts, and the useful range is small enough that changing it by a whole point is a visible edit.

No other model family reads the value, so the panel only shows the field once a Flux or Qwen Image model is selected, and leaves it out of the request otherwise.
generate.reference.karras.lead: Spaces the sampler's noise levels using the Karras schedule instead of the default one.
generate.reference.karras.body:
The schedule decides how much noise comes off at each step rather than how many steps there are. Karras spends more of them at the low-noise end, which often sharpens the result at low step counts and matters less as the count rises.

Some models are trained expecting it and some are not, and the panel reads the model's suggested schedulers to say which.

The horde's own default is off, and this form starts it on.
generate.reference.hires.lead: Renders at the model's native size first, then upscales that image and refines it.
generate.reference.hires.body:
Asking a model for a picture much larger than it was trained on is what produces two heads and three legs. At that scale it no longer knows what a whole body looks like, so it paints several.

The hires pass avoids this by generating small, where the model is competent, and repainting the enlarged version. It costs a second pass of time and kudos.

The panel suggests it when a Stable Diffusion 1.5 model is asked for more than 768 pixels on either side.
generate.reference.hires_denoise.lead: How much the hires pass is allowed to repaint the upscaled image.
generate.reference.hires_denoise.body: The second pass starts from the enlarged first render rather than from noise, and this decides how much of it survives. Low values keep the first pass's composition and mostly add sharpness; high values let the model add detail that was never there, and drift from the picture you were enlarging. It only reaches the request while the hires pass is on.
generate.reference.tiling.lead: Makes the edges of the image wrap, so copies laid side by side join without a seam.
generate.reference.tiling.body:
The model is asked to paint something whose left edge continues into its right and whose top continues into its bottom.

That is worth having for backgrounds, fabrics, ground textures and anything else meant to repeat, and of no use for a picture you are only going to look at once. It constrains the composition, so it is not free.

The examples show one render repeated nine times beside the tile on its own, because a seam only exists where one copy meets the next.
generate.reference.requirements.lead: The lines marked “Suggested” under a control come from the selected model's own reference entry.
generate.reference.requirements.body:
Model authors publish the steps, guidance, samplers, schedulers and CLIP skip their checkpoint was tuned for, and the panel shows those beside the fields they apply to.

They are recommendations, and nothing is enforced. A value the model was not tuned for is flagged, and the request is still sent exactly as you set it.

A model that publishes nothing shows no lines at all, which is not a statement that any value will do.
generate.reference.upscaler.lead: Enlarges the finished image with a dedicated upscaling model.
generate.reference.upscaler.body: It runs after generation, on the picture the model produced, so it changes nothing about the composition and cannot rescue a bad one. The plain and anime variants of RealESRGAN suit photographic and drawn work respectively. At most one upscaler runs, so picking a second replaces the first. It is a different tool from the hires pass, which enlarges mid-generation and repaints as it goes.
generate.reference.facefixer.lead: Runs a face restoration model over the result.
generate.reference.facefixer.body:
Small faces are where generation falls apart first: at a distance there are not enough pixels for the model to place eyes and a mouth convincingly.

GFPGAN and CodeFormers rebuild them from what a face is generally supposed to look like. That is also the catch, because what they know is faces in general rather than the one in your picture.

It does nothing for a face that is already large and correct.
generate.reference.facefixer_strength.le: How strongly the face fixer is applied.
generate.reference.facefixer_strength.bo: Low values are a touch-up and the original face still shows through; high values rebuild more of it, which clears up more damage and can leave every face in a batch looking related. It only reaches the request when a face fixer is actually selected, so moving it on its own does nothing.
generate.reference.strip_background.lead: Cuts the subject out of the finished image and leaves the background transparent.
generate.reference.strip_background.body:
It runs after generation, on the picture the model produced, so it changes nothing about the composition. What comes back is an image with the background gone rather than painted, which is what a sticker, a logo or anything meant to sit on another picture needs.

The remover decides for itself what the subject is, and it works on the whole picture rather than on anything you name. Hair, fur and thin edges are where the cut shows first, so a plain even background asked for in the prompt gives it a cleaner edge to find.

The same tool runs in alchemy on a picture you already have, which is where to send a render you have already made.
generate.reference.batch.lead: How many images this one request asks for.
generate.reference.batch.body: Each image is charged its own kudos and shares every setting apart from the seed, so a batch shows you several attempts at one prompt. That makes it the quickest way to find out whether a prompt is working, because a single disappointing result is often just an unlucky seed. QR-code requests are never batched, and each image in them is queued on its own.
generate.reference.nsfw.lead: Marks the request as possibly not safe for work, so only workers that accept those jobs pick it up.
generate.reference.nsfw.body: This says what the request may come back with. It does not check or filter the finished image. Leaving it off for a prompt that is plainly NSFW risks the job being rejected by a worker that did not sign up for it. Turning it on narrows the pool of workers willing to take the job, which can mean a longer wait.
generate.reference.censor_nsfw.lead: Asks workers to return a censored placeholder if the result trips their NSFW detector.
generate.reference.censor_nsfw.body: The check happens on the worker after the image has been generated, so this decides what comes back rather than what is made. It is on by default. It is a separate question from the NSFW flag, which is about which workers are willing to take the job at all: a request can be marked NSFW and still ask for a censored return.
generate.reference.trusted_workers.lead: Restricts the request to workers the horde has marked as trusted.
generate.reference.trusted_workers.body: Trust is earned by workers that have served a great deal of correct work, so the trusted pool is a small fraction of the network. The trade-off is simple: you know more about who runs your prompt, and you wait longer for it. It is off by default, which is the right setting for almost everything.
generate.reference.slow_workers.lead: Lets slower workers pick the request up.
generate.reference.slow_workers.body: It is on by default, and leaving it on usually gets you an image sooner, because more machines can take the job. Turning it off holds the request to faster hardware and costs more kudos for the same picture. Turn it off when you are waiting on something and want it now; leave it on the rest of the time.
generate.reference.extra_slow_workers.le: Also allows the slowest workers on the network to take the request.
generate.reference.extra_slow_workers.bo: These are the machines that would otherwise be filtered out entirely. It is worth turning on for an unpopular model that nothing else on the network is running, where a slow result beats no result. Expect the generation itself to take a long time. It is off by default.
generate.reference.allow_downgrade.lead: Lets the horde quietly reduce the request rather than refuse it when you cannot afford its full cost.
generate.reference.allow_downgrade.body: The reduction lands on the settings that carry the cost, such as the step count, so what comes back is a cheaper version of what you asked for rather than nothing at all. It is on by default, which suits anyone who would rather have an image than an error. Turn it off when you need the settings you set to be the settings that ran.
generate.reference.replacement_filter.le: Lets the horde replace words its filters flag instead of rejecting the whole request.
generate.reference.replacement_filter.bo: The horde runs prompts through filters, and this decides what happens when one fires: with it on the flagged wording is swapped and the request goes through, and with it off the request fails outright. It is on by default, here and on the horde's side. Turn it off if you want to know when a prompt is flagged. With it on, a flagged prompt is quietly changed, and you may not understand why the result differs from what you asked for.
generate.reference.webhook.lead: An http(s) address the horde POSTs each finished generation to.
generate.reference.webhook.body: It is for automation: a script or service of your own that would rather be told when an image is ready than poll for it. Leave it blank if you are only using this page. An address that does not parse as an http or https URL is dropped from the request rather than failing it, so a typo costs you the callback and nothing else.
generate.reference.workers.lead: Pins the request to named workers, or in avoid mode keeps those workers off it.
generate.reference.workers.body: At most five worker IDs are accepted. A short list usually means a longer wait, because only the machines on it can serve the request and they may be busy or offline. Avoid mode is the more useful half for most people: it routes around one worker that has been giving you bad results without narrowing the pool to almost nothing.
generate.reference.remember_extras.lead: Keeps the webhook URL and the worker list in this browser between visits.
generate.reference.remember_extras.body: Both can contain personal details, so they are cleared when you reload unless you turn this on. Everything else in the panel is remembered either way, including the QR text. Turn it on if you send every generation to the same webhook.
generate.reference.transparent.lead: Asks for an image with a transparent background rather than a painted one.
generate.reference.transparent.body: The transparency is produced during generation, so the edges are decided by the model as it paints rather than cut out afterwards. It needs a model and a worker that support it, and comes back opaque where they do not. It is not the same thing as the “Remove background” post-processor, which takes a finished image and cuts the subject out of it.
generate.reference.qr.lead: Weaves a scannable QR code carrying this text or URL into the image itself.
generate.reference.qr.body:
The code is part of the picture rather than pasted over it, so the prompt still decides what the image is of.

Ask for weather, vapour, foliage and light rather than blocks and hard shadows. The ControlNet already carries the code, and a prompt that describes geometry competes with it for the same pixels.

Beside the payload, the request can carry where the code sits, in pixels from the left and top edge, and which shape its squares are drawn as. Left alone, the workflow centres a square code.

Control strength says how closely the image follows the code, and the QR workflow takes it. Leave it unset and the request carries nothing for it, so the worker uses its own 1. The slider in the QR card sets it.

The examples on this page were made across that range on local software. Read them for what the range does to a code, and for how much of a scannable code comes from the prompt and its texture rather than from the number.

A few more things hold for every QR request:

- It needs a Stable Diffusion 1.5 or SDXL model.
- These requests are never batched, so each image in a batch is queued on its own.
- Leave the box blank and the workflow is not used at all.

generate.learn.flows.txt2img.steps.promp:
[[set:prompt]] is where you write what you want to see. Write it as a plain description:

- what the subject is
- where the subject is
- what the light and the mood are like

This example asked for `{{ prompt }}`.

[[set:negative]] names what you do not want in the picture. This one asked to avoid `{{ negative }}`.
[[set:prompt]] takes a plain description of subject, setting and light. This example asked for `{{ prompt }}`, and steered away from `{{ negative }}` in [[set:negative]].
generate.learn.flows.txt2img.steps.model:
A [[gl:model|model]] is the trained network that draws the picture.

Each model learned from a different set of images, so they differ in:

- the look they give a picture
- the subjects they handle well
- the way they read a prompt

This example used {{ model }}.
The [[gl:model|model]] is the checkpoint that draws the image; each carries its own trained look. This example used {{ model }}.
[[set:model]]: {{ model }}. SDXL, so native size is 1024.
[[set:size]] is the width and height of the picture in pixels.

A model is trained at one size and works less well away from it, so it pays to match. {{ model }} is an SDXL model, trained at {{ width }} by {{ height }}.

- Ask for much less and the framing collapses to a cramped close-up.
- Ask for much more and the model tends to draw the subject twice.
{{ width }}×{{ height }}, the native training size for an SDXL model like {{ model }}. Much less and the framing collapses; much more and subjects start duplicating.
[[set:size]] {{ width }}×{{ height }}: SDXL native. Much below it, detail collapses; much above it without hires fix, subjects duplicate.
generate.learn.flows.txt2img.steps.steps:
The model builds the picture in passes, tidying it a little each time. [[set:steps]] is how many passes it makes.

- Too few, and the image stays vague and smeared.
- Past a point, more passes change almost nothing and only cost you time and kudos.

This example used {{ steps }}.
[[set:steps]] {{ steps }}: the number of denoising passes. Under about twenty the image stays mushy, and well past forty you are mostly paying for nothing.
[[set:steps]]: {{ steps }}. Past the point where this model stops gaining structure; more adds texture, not structure.
generate.learn.flows.txt2img.steps.cfg.b:
[[set:cfg]] decides how hard the model is pushed to obey your words.

- Set it low and the model follows your words loosely, so the picture is pleasant but not quite what you asked for.
- Set it high and it follows you so literally that the colours go harsh and the picture looks overdone.

{{ cfg }} is a middle value that suits most prompts.
[[set:cfg]] is how tightly the model is held to the prompt. {{ cfg }} keeps it obedient without the burnt contrast you get higher up.
[[set:cfg]]: {{ cfg }}, Karras sigmas on. Below the point where the contrast burns.
generate.learn.flows.txt2img.steps.sampl:
[[set:sampler]] is the method used to turn the starting noise into a picture over those steps.

Samplers differ in how quickly the image settles and in how much the result varies between runs.

This example used {{ sampler }}, which is a dependable place to start.
[[set:sampler]] {{ sampler }}: an ancestral sampler, so it keeps injecting a little noise as it goes and stays varied. A safe default.
[[set:sampler]]: {{ sampler }}. Ancestral, so step count also re-rolls detail.
[[set:seed]] is the number the starting noise is generated from. The same seed with the same settings gives the same picture.

This example fixes it at {{ seed }}, which is what makes the example repeatable.

- Working on your own, leave it blank, so that every run gives you a fresh picture.
- Fix it once you have a picture you like and want to change one thing about it.

Leave it blank here and you get a picture like this one rather than this exact image.

[[set:seed]] {{ seed }}. A fixed seed is what makes a run repeatable.

Blank means a new seed every time you press Generate, which is the normal way to work until you have a picture worth refining.
[[set:seed]]: {{ seed }}, fixed so the example reproduces. Blank is the everyday setting; fix it to iterate on one result.

That is the whole request.

Press Generate and it joins a queue that volunteer workers pick jobs from, so your image arrives in anything from a few seconds to a few minutes.

It will not be identical to the example, and that is normal.
Send it. The job queues for a volunteer worker, so how long it takes depends on load and on how rare the model is.

Drag the slider. It starts at the first pass, where the picture is only random noise: a square of coloured speckle with no shapes in it. Every image starts here.

Each notch along the slider is one pass of the model. On every pass the model does the same job. It predicts which part of the picture is noise, and it removes some of it. That job is called denoising, and [[set:steps]] counts how many passes are made.

Halfway along you can make out shapes. By the last pass the noise is gone. The model never copies in an existing picture. Every pixel is the result of these passes.

Switch to "The model's guess" and you see what the model predicted the finished picture would be from that pass onward. Even an early prediction shows the right subject, which is why a half-finished picture looks rough and still looks like something.

Generating an image means denoising. A field of random noise goes through the model many times. Each pass predicts part of the noise and subtracts it, and what is left at the end is the picture. The model holds no stored images to fetch.
Iterative denoising from a random latent: each step predicts noise and removes a scheduled fraction of it, so the image is produced by the process and nothing is retrieved from storage.
How the prompt is used

Your prompt is used on every one of those passes. The words are converted into numbers, which is called conditioning, and they are given to the model again at each pass. They affect the picture the whole way through.

A prompt biases the picture. It is not a list of commands the model has to obey exactly. Three things follow from that:

- words near the start of the prompt have more effect
- repeating a word, or weighting it with [[set:prompt_emphasis]], gives it more effect
- anything you do not describe is still decided, and the model fills it with whatever was most common in its training images

Say it if you care about it.

[[set:negative]] works the same way in the opposite direction. What you write there biases the picture away from those things.

The prompt is encoded and used as conditioning on every step, so it shapes the picture the whole way through. Order and emphasis change the weighting, so terms near the front carry more. Anything you leave unstated is still decided, using whatever the model saw most of. [[set:negative]] conditions in the opposite direction.
Text conditioning is applied at every step, so token position and emphasis shift the whole trajectory. Unstated attributes fall to the prior, which is what makes a negative prompt worth writing.
What a model is

A model is a single large file. What it holds is numbers, called weights.

It was made by adding noise to millions of images that came with a text description, and training the network to remove that noise: the same job you just watched. The training images are not stored in the file.

What those numbers hold is a statistical average of how things usually look: the way light falls on skin, how the parts of a bicycle fit together. That is why a prompt describing something common gives a better picture than a prompt describing something rare.

Different [[gl:model|models]] were trained on different sets of images, which is why each one has its own look and its own strengths.

A [[gl:model|model]] is a file of weights: numbers fitted during training, with no copy of the training images in it. Training added noise to captioned images and taught the network to predict it, leaving a statistical sense of how things look. What a model was trained on is why one model draws better faces and another better landscapes.
Weights fitted to predict noise over captioned data. The training set's leanings are the model's style, which is why the baseline and the finetune move a result further than any single setting does.
Steps and guidance

Two settings decide how the passes you just watched are made.

[[set:steps]] is how many passes the model makes. Too few and the picture stays vague. Past a point the extra passes cost time and [[gl:kudos|kudos]] without changing much. The pictures on this page are the same request at step counts from 2 to 50.

[[set:cfg]], called guidance, sets how closely the picture is held to your words. Low, and the model has room to invent, so the picture is pleasant but may not be what you asked for. High, and every word is forced in, so the colours go harsh and the picture looks overdone. Between 5 and 10 suits most models.

The settings reference in these Learn pages gives the workable range for each.

[[set:steps]] is the count of denoising passes; [[set:cfg]] is how tightly the result is held to your words. Too few steps leaves the image unresolved, and high guidance makes the contrast harsh. The settings reference gives the workable range for both, with example pictures across the range.

Steps sets the schedule length, CFG the gap between the conditioned and unconditioned predictions. Both have a knee past which you pay without gaining, which is why the settings reference gives ranges rather than one number.
Why the same prompt gives a different picture

The starting noise is generated from a single number, and that number is [[set:seed]].

The same seed with the same model and settings gives the same image every time. A fresh seed gives a different picture from the same words, which is what the pictures here are, and why running a prompt again is a fair way to look for a better result.

That is also why the seed is normally left blank, and fixed only once you have a picture you want to refine.

[[set:sampler]] is the method that runs the passes. Some samplers add a small amount of fresh noise back at each pass. With those, changing the step count changes the picture itself, even with the seed fixed.

[[gl:worker|Workers]] across the horde also differ in hardware and software, so an exact match to someone else's image is not something to expect.

The starting noise comes from [[set:seed]]: fix it and a request reproduces, leave it blank and every submit re-rolls, which is the everyday setting. [[set:sampler]] is the method that runs the steps, and ancestral samplers keep adding noise back, so the detail moves when the step count does. Hardware and library versions differ between [[gl:worker|workers]] as well.
Seed fixes the initial latent, sampler fixes the path. Ancestral variants re-inject noise, so step count is not neutral there, and cross-worker determinism is not promised in any case.
Now make one

That is the whole process. An image starts as noise. The model removes the noise over a number of passes. Your prompt is applied on every pass. The seed, the step count and the guidance decide the rest.

The walkthrough goes through one real [[gl:request|request]] field by field and ends with you pressing Generate, which is the quickest way to make any of this stick.

Four parts: random noise to start from, a trained model that removes it, conditioning from your prompt applied at every step, and the settings that decide how many steps and how strictly. The walkthrough puts that into one real [[gl:request|request]], field by field.

generate.learn.flows.concepts_horde.step: Who generates your image

The AI Horde is a crowd of volunteers. Each one runs a small program called a worker on their own computer. The worker asks the horde for jobs and sends the finished images back. When you press Generate, someone's machine at home draws your picture. No company-owned servers are involved.

The number of workers rises and falls through the day as people switch them on and off, and so does the list of models you can pick from, because each worker chooses which models it carries.

The horde is a pool of volunteer-run workers, with no hosted service behind it. Each worker asks for jobs, generates, and returns the result. Capacity and the model list both move with who happens to be online, since workers choose what they carry.
A job broker over volunteer workers. Capacity and model availability track who is online, which is why the model list is fetched live.
What happens after you press Generate

Your request goes into the horde's queue, and no particular machine is chosen for it.

Workers ask for work as they free up, and one that carries your model and can meet what you asked for takes the job, generates the image, and sends it back for the horde to hand to you.

Where you sit in that queue depends on your kudos and on how ordinary the request is: a common model at a common size is picked up sooner than something only a couple of workers can serve.

Submitting puts the request in a shared queue. Workers poll it, and one matching the model and the request's requirements claims the job, generates, and returns the image. Queue position follows your kudos and how many workers can serve the request at all.
The request enters a shared queue; workers claim by capability match. Ordering is by kudos, and the count of workers able to serve it sets the floor on how fast anything moves.
What kudos are

Kudos are how the horde keeps track of who has given and who has taken.

- Running a worker and generating for other people earns them.
- Asking for images spends them.

Kudos cannot be bought, sold or exchanged for money, and they have no use outside the AI Horde. Their only effect is your place in the queue.

You can generate with none of them, or with a negative balance, and without an account at all. It only means waiting behind the people who have contributed.

Kudos are contribution accounting: earned by generating for others, spent by asking for images. They cannot be traded and have no use outside the horde. Their only effect is queue priority, so a low or negative balance costs you waiting and never access.
A priority ledger with no exchange outside the horde. There is no hard gate, so a negative balance costs latency and nothing else.
Trusted workers and the NSFW setting

The horde records how much correct work each worker has done. A worker that has served reliably for a long time is marked trusted.

You can ask that only trusted workers handle your requests, which usually means waiting longer for a smaller pool.

Every request also carries a flag saying whether it may come back with adult content. Workers set their own limits on what they will accept, so a request marked that way goes to the workers willing to serve it.

Both are options in the panel, and neither is worth thinking about on your first image.

Workers earn trust by serving reliably, and you can restrict a request to trusted ones at the cost of a smaller pool and a longer wait. The NSFW flag on a request is matched against what each worker is willing to accept. Both live in the horde section of the panel.

Trust is earned over served jobs; restricting to trusted workers narrows the pool and costs latency. The NSFW flag is matched against per-worker limits, so it routes the job and does not filter afterwards.
Why the wait moves around

How long you wait changes a lot from one request to the next. Four things decide it:

- how many workers are online at that moment
- how many people are queued ahead of you
- how rare the model you picked is
- how much work your request is to run

A large image with many steps takes a worker longer than a small one.

No fixed figure would be accurate. Watch the estimate the studio shows, and pick a common model when you are in a hurry.

The wait depends on how many workers are online, how deep the queue ahead of you is, how many workers carry your model, and how much work the request is (size and steps). None of that is fixed, so what the studio shows is an estimate. A common model at a common size is the fastest thing to ask for.
Latency follows live worker count, queue depth ahead of you, model availability and the request's own cost. All four move, so the estimate is an estimate.
What you get back

When a worker finishes, the picture comes straight back to you and lands in the results panel as a tile. Open one to see it larger, or use its menu to reuse the settings that made it, send it back in as a source image, or download it.

The horde keeps no copy. Your finished images are held in this browser and nowhere else, so download anything you want to keep.

Finished images come back as tiles in the results panel. Open one for a larger view; its menu reuses the settings that made it, sends the picture back in as a source, or downloads it. The horde keeps no copy, so results live in this browser alone and anything you want to keep has to be downloaded.

Results come back to the browser and are held there rather than on the horde. A tile's menu reuses its settings, sends it back as a source image, or downloads it. Nothing survives clearing the browser's stored data.
See it for yourself

You can check all of this yourself.

The Workers page lists every machine signed in right now, what it carries and how much it has generated, and the Status page shows the queue and how much work the horde is getting through.

The Workers page lists who is online and what they carry, and the Status page shows the current queue and throughput. The walkthrough takes one request through the panel and into that queue.
Workers and Status show the live pool and the queue. The walkthrough runs one committed request through the panel.
