If you have generated images in another program, you already know most of these controls. [[set:prompt]] and [[set:negative]] are the two boxes you expect, and [[set:steps]] is steps. [[set:cfg]] is what some tools label guidance: how firmly the model is held to your words.

[[set:sampler]] lists the same k_ names you have been choosing between. [[set:seed]] is the number the starting noise comes from, and [[set:denoise]], on a request that starts from your own picture, is how much of that picture is allowed to change.

Two controls are in a different place here, though they do the same job. [[set:hires]] is a switch with its own strength slider, in the Size card, where in most tools it is one control. [[set:clip_skip]] sits in the Sampling card and is set per request, where most tools set it once in a settings page.

The example pictures here show them working, so you can see they do what you expect before you rely on them. Every field's reference page names the API field behind it, so if you know a setting by its API name you can find it that way too.

Your vocabulary carries over. [[set:prompt]], [[set:negative]], [[set:steps]], [[set:cfg]] (guidance, in the tools that call it that), [[set:sampler]] with the same k_ names, [[set:seed]], and [[set:denoise]] on a request that starts from a picture all mean here what they mean everywhere else. [[set:model]] and [[set:loras]] are where you would look for them.

Two have moved. [[set:hires]] is a toggle paired with its own denoising slider in the Size card, and [[set:clip_skip]] is a per-request field under Sampling. Both have example pictures here so you can see them behaving as you would expect. Each reference page names the API field, which is the fastest way to place anything you cannot find by its label.
Same parameter set, same names, API field on every reference page. Two to relearn: [[set:hires]] is a toggle plus a paired denoise under Size, and [[set:clip_skip]] is per-request under Sampling.

The big difference is where the work happens.

Nothing runs on your computer. The request goes to the [[gl:ai_horde|AI Horde]], a volunteer's machine somewhere picks it up, draws the picture and sends it back. That is why there is no progress bar. What you watch instead is your place in the queue and how fast the [[gl:worker|worker]] that took the job happens to be.

[[gl:kudos|Kudos]] are the other new idea. They record who has given and who has taken: running a worker for other people earns them, asking for images spends them. They set your place in the queue and nothing else, so generating is free, and works with no kudos, a negative balance, or no account at all.

The [[set:model]] list shows what the workers online right now are carrying. It changes on its own, there is nothing for you to download, and a model you used yesterday may be missing this evening. Picking a common model means many workers can take your job and it comes back sooner.

Model authors publish the sampler, [[set:karras]] setting and [[set:clip_skip]] their model was tuned for. The panel shows those as suggestions beside each of those controls.

One habit to change: a fixed [[set:seed]] does not guarantee the same picture here. It fixes the starting noise, but workers run different hardware and different library versions, so the same seed on a different worker gives a slightly different picture. The example pictures here show the everyday case, the same request re-rolled.

There is no fixed hardware behind this. Your request enters a shared queue, a volunteer-run [[gl:worker|worker]] claims it, generates, and returns the result. In place of a local progress bar you watch two numbers that are not about your machine: your queue position and that worker's speed. [[gl:kudos|Kudos]] are contribution accounting, earned by generating for others and spent by asking, and their only effect is queue priority: a zero or negative balance costs waiting and never access.

The [[set:model]] list is whatever the online workers carry, so it changes as they come and go. A model few workers carry means a longer wait, so the choice affects speed as well as look. Models carry reference entries naming the sampler, schedule and clip skip they were tuned for, and the panel shows those beside the controls they apply to.

Determinism is per worker. The [[set:seed]] fixes the starting noise, but hardware and library versions vary across the pool, so reproducing an image exactly is not something to plan around. The example pictures show the ordinary case, one request re-rolled.

A job broker over volunteer workers, with no local runtime: queue position and the claiming worker's throughput stand in for a progress bar. [[gl:kudos|Kudos]] set priority and gate nothing. The [[set:model]] list is the union of what online workers carry, and reference entries drive the inline sampler, [[set:karras]] and [[set:clip_skip]] suggestions. Cross-worker determinism is not promised: the [[set:seed]] fixes the latent, the pool varies the rest.

Some controls from your old program have no equivalent here, and they are not planned.

Custom schedulers, extension scripts and add-ons belong to that program. A request sent to the horde has to be something any matching worker can run, so the panel offers only the settings every worker understands.

There is also no model folder to manage, no download button and no disk space to watch, because you never hold the model. There is no local progress bar either, because the picture is drawn somewhere else.

If you go looking for one of these and cannot find it, you have not missed it.

Anything outside the horde's request schema has no field. Bespoke schedulers, extension scripts and per-tool add-ons stay with the tool that owns them, since any matching worker has to be able to serve the request. What the panel offers is the common ground every worker understands. Model files, downloads and disk are also absent, because the model lives on the worker.
The horde's request schema is the limit of what any client can send. Bespoke schedulers, extension scripts and tool-specific add-ons have no field, and nothing about model storage is yours to manage.

That is the summary. The controls are the same and mostly keep their names. Someone else's machine does the work, so you watch a queue position in place of a progress bar, and the model list is whatever the volunteers are running.

generate.control_types.head: Control types
generate.control_types.lead: Each control type reads something different from your picture: its edges, its depth, a pose, its colours. This page shows what each one keeps and what it lets the model change. Press any control type to see it on three pictures, and to see what changes as you raise the control strength.
generate.control_types.body: The image you get back is not a copy of your picture. A detector reads your picture first and draws a control map from it: outlines, a clean line drawing, how far away each part is, which way each surface faces, where the joints of a body are, or flat colour fields. The worker then makes a new image that follows that map. So choosing a control type is choosing what has to survive from your picture.
generate.control_types.worlds: Each control type here is shown on three pictures, because what a detector keeps depends on what it is given. Press one to see all three. For each you get the picture it started from, the control map the detector drew, and the image that map guided. Everything else is the same across all of them: one model, one prompt, one seed, one control strength.
generate.control_types.group_edges: These read the outlines of your picture. The image keeps the same shapes, and the colour, the material and the style can all change.
generate.control_types.group_lines: These draw your picture as clean lines. The ones that keep straight lines only leave you the architecture and drop everything curved.
generate.control_types.group_depth: These read how far each part of your picture is from the camera. The image keeps the same arrangement in space, and the drawing itself can change.
generate.control_types.group_surface: These read which way each surface faces. The image keeps the same modelling and light, and the model redraws the picture.
generate.control_types.group_pose: These read the people and nothing else. The same stance comes back in any setting.
generate.control_types.group_regions: These read your picture as flat fields, one for each kind of thing. The image keeps the same layout, and every surface is redrawn.
generate.control_types.group_colour: These read the palette or the tones. The tile readers read the picture itself, which is how you add detail to it or enlarge it under guidance.

alchemy.usecases.describe.lead: Reads an image and answers with words, tags or numbers instead of another image.
alchemy.usecases.describe.body: Each form takes the same source image and returns different kinds of responses: a one-line caption, a tag list, a safety verdict, a colour palette. Several can run on one submission, so a single upload can come back captioned, tagged and rated at once. Each operation is charged separately, but the horde runs them at the same time and returns them together.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.title: Extract a control map
alchemy.usecases.control_map.note: Read the structure of a picture: its outlines, how far away each part is, or where the joints of a body are. The result is another picture, called a control map, which can guide a later image. These also have other artistic uses, as line art to colour in, a depth relief, or flat colour regions to cut a mask from.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.lead: Reads the structure of a picture and returns a new picture of that structure.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.gallery_lea: All the examples are based on this image.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.pick: Which one to pick depends on what you want kept. Edges and line art hold the outlines, so a new image redraws the same shapes in another style. Depth and surface direction hold the layout in space and let the drawing go. Pose holds the people and nothing else. Regions give flat fields to work from, either as a plan for a new image or as a mask for another tool. Colour and texture keep the palette or the tones, and the tile detectors keep the picture itself, which is how detail is added or a picture enlarged under guidance.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.map_alt: {{ detector }} control map of the source
alchemy.usecases.control_map.group_edges: Outlines and the boundaries between light and dark. Canny is thin and literal. The soft-edge detectors follow the shapes a person would draw and ignore fine texture. The scribble detectors draw deliberately rough lines.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.group_lines: Clean line drawings, the way an illustrator would ink the picture. mlsd keeps the straight segments only, which is usually the architecture.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.group_depth: How far each part of the picture is from the camera, drawn light for near and dark for far.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.group_surfa: Which way each surface faces, drawn as colour.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.group_pose: The people in the picture, drawn as skeletons and nothing else.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.group_regio: The picture divided into flat fields, one colour for each kind of thing.
alchemy.usecases.control_map.group_colou: These keep the palette or the tones of your picture, and let the shapes go. The tile detectors keep the picture itself, as a guide for redrawing it.
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.title: Enlarge a picture
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.note: Run an upscaler over the image. Which one to pick depends on whether the source is a photograph, artwork or animation.
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.lead: Redraws the image at two or four times its size, filling in detail the original never had.
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.body: An upscaler is a model, and what it was trained on decides what it invents in the gaps. The photographic models keep skin and fabric plausible, while the anime models keep line art crisp instead of smearing it into gradients. The badge on each row is the factor that model enlarges by. Vectorize is in this group but has no badge, because it does not enlarge the picture. It redraws it as shapes and saves it as an SVG, a format that stays sharp at any size.
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.title: Repair faces
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.note: Rebuild faces a generator got wrong. Most useful on small or distant faces, which is where models fail first.
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.lead: Finds faces in the image and redraws them, which is the usual repair for the melted features small renders produce.
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.body: GFPGAN rebuilds a face aggressively, and will replace one that was already nearly correct. CodeFormers keeps more of the original and is the safer choice on a portrait you mostly like. Running either over a face that was already correct still changes it, so use one only where a face needs repair.
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.title: Cut out the background (rembg)
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.note: Remove everything behind the subject and return the image with transparency.
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.lead: Separates the subject from its background and returns a transparent cutout of what is left.
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.body: The cut follows whatever the model takes to be the subject, so one clear subject cuts well and a crowd or a soft edge does not. The result carries an alpha channel, which is why it appears over a checkerboard in some viewers and over nothing at all in others.

alchemy.form_meta.vectorize.desc: Converts the image into a scalable SVG vector graphic.

alchemy.form_meta.aesthetic.desc: Rates the image on a 0-10 aesthetic scale using the LAION aesthetic predictor. Higher is more visually appealing.
alchemy.form_meta.GFPGAN.desc: Fast, general-purpose face restoration. A good default; makes only subtle changes to identity.
alchemy.form_meta.GFPGAN.example: Result: Sharper facial features, reduced blur, improved skin texture while preserving identity
alchemy.form_meta.GFPGANv1.3.desc: An earlier GFPGAN version, kept for compatibility. Slightly softer results than current GFPGAN.
alchemy.form_meta.GFPGANv1.3.example: Result: Softer facial restoration with subtle improvements to clarity
alchemy.form_meta.CodeFormers.desc: Stronger restoration for badly damaged or very low-resolution faces. Can alter identity or fine details more than GFPGAN.
alchemy.form_meta.CodeFormers.example: Result: Aggressive face reconstruction, best for severely degraded images but may change fine details
alchemy.form_meta.RestoreFormer.desc: Favours fidelity to the original face over aggressive fixing, a gentler alternative to CodeFormers.
alchemy.form_meta.RestoreFormer.example: Result: Conservative restoration that maintains original facial characteristics
alchemy.form_meta.RealESRGAN_x2plus.desc: General-purpose upscaler for real photos, a more conservative size increase.
alchemy.form_meta.RealESRGAN_x4plus_anim: Tuned for anime and illustrated line art.
alchemy.form_meta.NMKD_Siax.desc: Sharp detail recovery, suited to photos and fine textures.
alchemy.form_meta.4x_AnimeSharp.desc: A sharpened upscaler for anime and illustrations.
alchemy.form_meta.4xNomos8kSC.desc: Trained on high-resolution photos; strong fine-detail sharpening.
alchemy.form_meta.4xLSDIRplus.desc: General-purpose photo upscaler tuned for natural, balanced detail.
alchemy.form_meta.4xNomosWebPhoto_RealPL: Tuned for photos sourced from the web; handles compression artifacts well.
alchemy.form_meta.4xNomos2_realplksr_dys: A newer Nomos model with smoother detail reconstruction.
alchemy.form_meta.4xNomos2_hq_dat2.desc: A higher-quality Nomos variant for already-clean source photos.
alchemy.form_meta.strip_background.desc: Removes the background entirely, leaving a transparent cutout of the main subject.
alchemy.form_meta.annotation.desc: Extracts the selected structure, such as edges, depth, or pose, and returns the map used to guide a ControlNet request.
alchemy.form_meta.annotation.example: Example: canny returns an edge map; depth returns a grayscale depth estimate.
alchemy.annotation.detector_label: What to read from the picture
alchemy.annotation.none_picked: Pick at least one detector, or turn the control map off.
alchemy.annotation.detector_hint: Each detector reads a different kind of structure, so the same picture gives a different guidance image for each one. Pick as many as you want and one map comes back per detector.
alchemy.annotation.detector_gallery: See every detector run on the same picture
alchemy.annotation.detector.canny: Finds hard outlines a pixel wide wherever light meets dark. It makes no distinction between the edge of an object and the edge of a texture, so a detailed photograph gives a busy map.
alchemy.annotation.detector.hed: Reads soft edges, following the shapes a person would trace rather than every hard boundary, which suits a photograph better than canny does.
alchemy.annotation.detector.pidinet: Reads soft edges like hed, thinner and cleaner, and runs quicker.
alchemy.annotation.detector.teed: The newest of the soft edge readers, with thin continuous lines and less speckle than hed or pidinet.
alchemy.annotation.detector.pyracanny: Runs canny over several sizes of your picture at once, so the large shapes survive and the fine texture drops out.
alchemy.annotation.detector.binary: Turns everything darker than a threshold black and the rest white, with no edge finding at all, so it wants a stark drawing to start from.
alchemy.annotation.detector.scribble: Traces the dark parts of your picture coarsely, on purpose, and expects a drawing on a pale ground; on a photograph use fakescribbles.
alchemy.annotation.detector.fakescribble: Thins the soft edge map down to a loose hand-drawn scribble, which is the one to use on a photograph.
alchemy.annotation.detector.scribble_xdo: Draws a scribble from the difference between two blurs, with finer strokes than the plain scribble and more of the faint detail kept.
alchemy.annotation.detector.scribble_pid: Thins pidinet's edges to a scribble, cleaner and more continuous than the other scribbles.
alchemy.annotation.detector.standard_lin: Calculates a plain ink drawing directly from the pixels, with no model involved. It is fast, and it loses faint detail.
alchemy.annotation.detector.lineart: Traces a photograph the way an illustrator would ink it, with weighted strokes and the faintest detail left out.
alchemy.annotation.detector.lineart_anim: Draws the lines in the anime idiom, with even strokes and closed shapes ready to be coloured in.
Draws anime lines after cleaning out paper grain and screentone, which suits scans and heavily compressed pictures.
alchemy.annotation.detector.mlsd: Keeps straight line segments only and discards everything curved, which usually leaves the architecture.
alchemy.annotation.detector.depth: Reads how far away each part of your picture is. It is reliable across a whole scene, though it loses small objects.
alchemy.annotation.detector.midas_depth: The older and faster depth map, coarser than the rest and steady on an ordinary photograph.
alchemy.annotation.detector.zoe_depth: Reads depth in real distances rather than relative ones, so near and far stay in proportion across the picture.
alchemy.annotation.detector.depth_anythi: A newer depth map that holds fine detail: hair, railings, leaves.
The sharpest depth map on offer, with cleaner boundaries between objects and less smearing than depth_anything.
alchemy.annotation.detector.normal: Works out which way each surface faces from a depth map, rougher than normal_bae and tolerant of an odd picture.
alchemy.annotation.detector.normal_bae: Reads which way each surface faces with a model trained for it, the cleaner of the two and the usual pick.
alchemy.annotation.detector.openpose: Draws the people as skeletons, with body, hands and face as coloured sticks and dots on black, and discards everything else.
alchemy.annotation.detector.seg: Splits your picture into flat coloured fields, one colour for each kind of thing, in the quick and coarse version.
alchemy.annotation.detector.oneformer_ad: The same split done by a stronger model over a scenery vocabulary: walls, sky, floor, furniture, plants.
alchemy.annotation.detector.oneformer_co: The same split over an object vocabulary, which names people, animals and things carried or sat on rather than the parts of a room.
alchemy.annotation.detector.color: Reduces your picture to a grid of flat colour blocks, keeping the palette and where each colour sits, and nothing of the drawing.
alchemy.annotation.detector.shuffle: Distorts your picture into a swirl. The colours and textures are kept, and the composition is destroyed. Use it to pass on a picture's palette and feel without its layout.
alchemy.annotation.detector.recolor_lumi: Makes a greyscale copy, weighted the way the human eye judges brightness. Use it as the map when you want to change a picture's colours but keep its shading.
alchemy.annotation.detector.recolor_inte: Makes a grey copy from the strongest colour channel, which leaves saturated colours brighter than the luminance version does.
alchemy.annotation.detector.tile: Blurs your picture to its broad shapes, which is what a tile ControlNet needs to add detail without inventing a different picture.
alchemy.annotation.detector.tile_ttplane: A gentler tile map that blurs the flat areas and leaves the edges crisp, and the steadier one on a photograph.
The plain tile map, an even blur with no edges kept, quicker and enough when your picture is already clean.

alchemy.dev.flow.heading: The general flow
alchemy.dev.flow.submit_desc: POST your source image and chosen forms to the async endpoint. You get back a request id.
alchemy.dev.flow.poll_desc: Poll the status endpoint with that id (this page polls every 10 seconds) until the overall state is 'done' and every form has finished, in state `done` or `faulted`.
alchemy.dev.flow.read_desc: Each form carries its own result: text and data inline, or a presigned image URL. Those URLs expire after about 30 minutes, so download them promptly. This studio does that for you and keeps the bytes in your browser.
alchemy.dev.flow.cancel_desc: DELETE the same status URL to cancel; any forms that already finished are still returned.

alchemy.dev.request.desc: POST a JSON body with the forms you want and the image to process.
alchemy.dev.request.source_note: source_image accepts either a publicly reachable image URL or a bare base64-encoded image (no data: prefix). Invalid or oversized images are rejected at submit time.
alchemy.dev.status.heading: Reading the status
alchemy.dev.status.desc: The status response reports an overall state plus a per-form breakdown. A form's result appears once its state is 'done'.
alchemy.dev.status.result_note: Data forms return their values inline. Post-processor forms key the form name to a time-limited, presigned image URL. The overall state can read 'done' while a slower form is still processing, so keep polling until every form is terminal.
alchemy.dev.sdk.heading: Using the SDK
alchemy.dev.sdk.desc: Rather than calling the endpoints by hand, the official horde-sdk Python library wraps the whole submit-and-poll cycle with typed models. The alchemy example walks through a complete request end to end.

workers.what_are.title: What Are Workers?
workers.what_are.description: Workers are volunteer-run software that process AI generation requests for the Horde. They poll the [[gl:ai_horde|AI Horde]] API for pending [[gl:job|jobs]], generate results using your GPU, and return them to the requesting user. In return, you earn [[gl:kudos|kudos]], the Horde's priority currency.
workers.what_are.types_intro: There are three types of workers: [[gl:dreamer|Dreamers]] generate images, [[gl:scribe|Scribes]] produce text, and [[gl:alchemist|Alchemists]] handle post-processing tasks like upscaling and captioning. Each worker loads one or more [[gl:model|models]], the trained AI files that determine what it can generate.
workers.diagram.aria_label: Diagram showing how AI Horde workers process requests: a user submits a request to the API, a worker polls for and processes the job, then returns the result
workers.diagram.intro: AI Horde works as a request loop. Users talk to the API, and workers repeatedly poll the API for jobs they can run.
workers.diagram.loop_hint: This cycle repeats continuously — workers never accept inbound jobs, they always ask the API for the next one.

workers.faq.title: Our Guarantees to Workers
workers.faq.privacy.title: User Privacy
workers.faq.privacy.description: Workers never receive any identifying information about the user who submitted a request. All requests are anonymized by the API before being dispatched to workers.
workers.faq.security.title: Network Security
workers.faq.security.description: Workers only make outbound connections to poll the API for jobs. They never listen on ports or accept incoming connections, so running a worker does not expose your system to the internet.
workers.faq.trust.title: Trust System
workers.faq.trust.description: The Horde uses a trust and suspicion system to protect against abuse. Workers that consistently deliver quality results build trust, while those producing bad outputs are flagged and eventually excluded.
workers.faq.cost.title: Obligations
workers.faq.cost.description: You volunteer your GPU when it's idle and stop whenever you want. There are no costs or obligations to run a worker, and you can uninstall the software at any time. You can recover the effort you put in by spending kudos.

help.workers.title: What are Workers?
help.workers.subtitle: Volunteer GPUs powering the AI Horde network
help.workers.body:
[[gl:worker|Workers]] are volunteer computers (typically with powerful GPUs) that process AI generation requests for the entire [[gl:ai_horde|AI Horde]] community. Anyone with a compatible GPU can run worker software to contribute processing power.

There are three types: [[gl:dreamer|Image workers (Dreamers)]] generate images, [[gl:scribe|Text workers (Scribes)]] generate text, and [[gl:alchemist|Alchemy workers (Alchemists)]] handle image utilities like captioning and upscaling. Each worker loads one or more [[gl:model|models]], the trained AI files that determine what it can generate.

This page shows all currently online workers, their performance, loaded models, and capabilities. Workers earn [[gl:kudos|kudos]] for their owners as a reward for volunteering.
help.models.title: What are Models?
help.models.subtitle: The AI brains that power each generation
help.models.body:
Models are trained AI files that workers load to generate images or text. Different models specialize in different styles, quality levels, and capabilities: for example, some excel at photorealism while others are better at anime or illustration.

The Workers column shows how many volunteer GPUs currently have this model loaded and ready. Queued shows the amount of pending work waiting. ETA is the estimated time to clear the queue. Performance shows the current generation speed across all workers running that model.

More workers on a model means faster generation times and lower queue wait times for users requesting that model.
help.stats.title: Usage Statistics
help.stats.subtitle: Real-time and historical performance of the AI Horde
help.stats.body:
This page shows the current state and historical usage of the entire AI Horde distributed network. The Overview tab shows real-time generation speeds, active worker counts, and current queue sizes.

Standard images are a normalized unit: one standard image equals a typical 1024×1024 image at 20 steps. Pages of text normalize token counts into roughly 500-word pages. These units make it easier to understand the scale of work being done.

The Image and Text tabs show per-model breakdowns, indicating which models are most popular and how the workload is distributed across available models.
help.workers.tooltip.total_workers: The number of volunteer machines currently online and processing requests for this worker type.
help.workers.tooltip.total_threads: Total parallel processing slots across all workers. A worker with 2 threads can process 2 jobs simultaneously.
help.workers.tooltip.performance: Total capacity: the combined average speed of all online workers. These averages represent the speed over the past several jobs. The actual output (Recent Throughput) is usually higher due to differences in speed between different models and parameters.
help.workers.tooltip.recent_throughput: Recent throughput: actual work the network completed in the last 60 seconds. This is the same number shown on the homepage and reflects real output, not just average worker performance.
help.workers.tooltip.capabilities: Special features this worker supports beyond basic generation. Not all workers support all capabilities.
help.workers.tooltip.worker_id: A unique identifier (UUID) for this worker. Useful for looking up a specific worker or reporting issues.
help.workers.tooltip.bridge_agent: The software connecting this volunteer's GPU to the AI Horde network. Different bridges may support different features.
help.workers.tooltip.threads: How many jobs this worker can process in parallel. More threads means higher throughput but requires more GPU memory.
help.workers.tooltip.models_loaded: AI models currently loaded on this worker. Workers with more models can handle a wider variety of requests but use more memory.
help.workers.tooltip.img2img: Supports image-to-image generation: creating new images based on an input image and a text prompt.
help.workers.tooltip.inpainting: Supports inpainting: selectively regenerating parts of an image while keeping the rest intact.
help.workers.tooltip.post_processing: Supports post-processing effects like upscaling, face fixing (GFPGAN/CodeFormers), and other image enhancements.
help.workers.tooltip.lora: Supports LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): small add-on models that modify generation style without replacing the base model.
help.workers.tooltip.controlnet: Supports ControlNet: advanced guidance that uses reference images (edges, poses, depth maps) to control generation composition.
help.workers.tooltip.sdxl_controlnet: Supports ControlNet specifically for SDXL (Stable Diffusion XL) models.
help.workers.tooltip.nsfw: Whether this worker accepts requests marked as NSFW (Not Safe For Work). Workers with NSFW disabled will skip such requests.
help.workers.tooltip.maintenance: Worker is temporarily offline for maintenance by its owner. It will not accept new jobs until maintenance is cleared.
help.workers.tooltip.paused: Worker has been paused by a moderator and cannot accept jobs until unpaused.
help.workers.tooltip.flagged: Worker has been flagged by moderators for investigation, typically due to suspicious output or behavior.
help.workers.tooltip.trusted: Worker owner has been verified as trusted; they've run a worker reliably for at least one week.
help.stats.tooltip.realtime_performance: Live generation speeds measured across all currently active workers in the network.
help.stats.tooltip.queued_requests: Total user requests waiting to be processed. Each request may contain multiple individual jobs.
help.stats.tooltip.queued_work: The total volume of pending work, measured in native units (megapixelsteps for images, tokens for text).
help.stats.tooltip.worker_count: Number of volunteer machines currently running and connected to the AI Horde network.
help.glossary.title: AI Horde Glossary
help.glossary.controls_heading: Buttons and marks on this page
help.glossary.controls_note: What the studio shows without words beside it.
help.glossary.controls.presets.title: Saved presets
help.glossary.controls.presets.body: Opens the saved presets. A preset stores every setting on this panel so you can come back to it, and the same menu keeps the last few requests you sent.
help.glossary.controls.reset.title: Start over
help.glossary.controls.reset.body: Puts every setting back where it started. It asks first, so a stray press cannot clear a panel you spent a while on.
help.glossary.controls.request_view.body: Shows the request the studio would send, written the way the API reads it. Handy for repeating a generation from your own code.
help.glossary.controls.panel_size.title: Widen the panel
help.glossary.controls.panel_size.body: Gives the settings more of the screen and the results less. Press it again to hand the room back.
help.glossary.controls.help.title: Help
help.glossary.controls.help.body: Opens this glossary. It opens on whichever studio you are in, so what it offers you is about the panel in front of you.
help.glossary.controls.prompt_expand.bod: Opens the prompt in a full-size editor. Nothing about the prompt changes; you just get more of the screen to read it in.
help.glossary.controls.prompt_history.bo: Lists the prompts you have written before on this machine. Picking one puts it back in the box.
help.glossary.controls.style_clear.title: Clear the style
help.glossary.controls.style_clear.body: Drops the style you picked. Any setting the style was holding becomes yours to change again.
help.glossary.controls.seed_random.title: New seed
help.glossary.controls.seed_random.body: Rolls a fresh seed, so the next image starts from different noise. Keep a seed instead and the same request makes the same image.
help.glossary.controls.lint.title: Checks on your request
help.glossary.controls.lint.body: Counts the things worth a second look before you generate. None of them stops the request; press the count to read what they are.
help.glossary.controls.select_images.bod: Turns the results into a list you can tick, so one download or one delete covers everything you chose.
help.glossary.controls.tile_actions.body: Opens what you can do with one image: save it, send it to alchemy, copy its settings back into the panel, or throw it away.
help.glossary.controls.tile_prompt.title: Show the prompt
help.glossary.controls.tile_prompt.body: Unfolds the prompt an image was made from, on the image itself.
help.glossary.controls.viewer_nav.title: Next and previous
help.glossary.controls.viewer_nav.body: Steps to the image before or after this one while one is open large.
help.glossary.controls.source_clear.body: Takes the picture back out of the request, so the panel goes back to making images from the prompt alone.
help.glossary.controls.close.title: Close
help.glossary.controls.close.body: Closes whatever is open over the page. On an image still being made, it cancels that request instead.
help.glossary.controls.section_chip.body: The small coloured mark beside a card's name. Every part of the panel has its own mark and colour, and a warning about that part wears the same one.
help.glossary.controls.style_lock.title: Held by a style
help.glossary.controls.style_lock.body: A padlock on a value means the style you picked is setting it. Choose “Use my values” beside it to take the setting back.
help.glossary.controls.retry_badge.title: Tried again
help.glossary.controls.retry_badge.body: A count on an image means the studio asked the horde again after a worker dropped the job. It is still the same request, not a new one.
help.glossary.controls.tutorial_door.bod: A card wearing the amber cap starts a walkthrough: it sets the panel up a step at a time and says why each step is there.
help.glossary.controls.studio_door.title: Try it card
help.glossary.controls.studio_door.body: A card wearing this mark carries a setting into the panel for you. The “See it in action” cards do the same, and show the setting changing first.
help.glossary.page_no_results: Nothing on this page matches that.
help.glossary.terms.scheduler.title: Scheduler
help.glossary.terms.scheduler.body: The plan for how much noise comes out at each step. It works with the sampler rather than instead of it, and the same prompt under two schedulers lands in slightly different places.
help.glossary.terms.sampler_settings.bod: The fine dials a few samplers accept: how much fresh noise is added back at each step, how far a step is allowed to wander, and which solver a multi-step sampler uses. Left alone they take the sampler's own defaults, which is where most requests should leave them.
help.glossary.terms.sampler_tier.title: Work per step
help.glossary.terms.sampler_tier.body: Some samplers walk the path twice or three times for every step you ask for. The tier beside a sampler's name says how much work one of its steps really is, and the kudos estimate charges for it.
help.glossary.terms.batch.title: Batch
help.glossary.terms.batch.body: How many images one press of Generate asks for. Each one is a separate job on a worker, and they can come back in any order.
help.glossary.terms.style.title: Style
help.glossary.terms.style.body: A named bundle of settings someone published: a prompt shape, a model, and usually a sampler and size to go with it. Picking one holds those settings until you take them back.
help.glossary.terms.preset.title: Preset
help.glossary.terms.preset.body: Your own copy of the whole panel, saved under a name. Unlike a style it is private to this browser, and it stores every setting rather than a chosen few.
help.glossary.terms.lint.title: Checks
help.glossary.terms.lint.body: The studio's own reading of your request before it is sent: settings that fight each other, values a model will ignore, costs worth knowing about. They are advice, and none of them blocks a request.
help.glossary.terms.baseline.title: Baseline
help.glossary.terms.baseline.body: The family a model was built on, such as Stable Diffusion 1.5, SDXL or Flux. Sizes, samplers and extras like ControlNet all depend on the baseline rather than on the individual model.
help.glossary.terms.temporary_link.title: Temporary image link
help.glossary.terms.temporary_link.body: Finished images are handed over as a link that expires after a short while rather than kept for you. Save anything you want to keep; the studio also keeps a copy in this browser until you clear it.
help.glossary.terms.control_map.title: Control map
help.glossary.terms.control_map.body: A picture of an image's structure rather than its colours: its edges, its depth, or the pose in it. Alchemy makes one, and a generation can then be held to that structure with ControlNet.
help.glossary.page.profile.requests_made: Requests made to the horde by this account.
help.glossary.page.profile.requests_fulf: Number of requests this account's workers have fulfilled.
help.glossary.page.profile.total_fulfill: The combined total number of requests this account's workers have fulfilled.
help.glossary.page.profile.kudos_generat: Generated work from this account's workers, shown as megapixelsteps (and tokens in detailed records).
help.glossary.page.profile.accumulated.d: Generated kudos earned by this account over its lifetime. API field: `kudos_details.accumulated`.
help.glossary.page.profile.gifted.descri: Kudos transferred to other users. API field: `kudos_details.gifted`.
help.glossary.page.profile.received.desc: Kudos received through transfers from other users. API field: `kudos_details.received`.
help.glossary.page.profile.recurring.des: Kudos generated by the system as a result of cash donations you make to help run the service. Certain volunteers also receive these kudos, such as moderators. API field: `kudos_details.recurring`.
help.glossary.page.profile.donated.descr: Kudos transferred to public-good keys, such as Educational Accounts. API field: `kudos_details.donated`.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_type_ima: Worker specializes in image generation tasks. These workers typically run software like reGen and support models such as Stable Diffusion.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_type_tex: Worker specializes in text generation tasks. These workers typically run software like KoboldCpp or Aphrodite and support various LLM models.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_type_int: Worker specializes in post-processing tasks such as image upscaling, face fixing, captioning, and interrogation. These workers typically run the AI-Horde-Worker bridge.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_online.d: Worker is online and is available for processing jobs.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_issue.de: Worker may be experiencing issues affecting its performance.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_issue_ma: Worker is in maintenance mode and will not accept new jobs.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_issue_pa: Worker has been paused by a moderator due to suspicious activity.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_issue_fl: Worker has been flagged by moderators for policy violations.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_issue_mu: Worker has multiple active issues. Review the status indicators for details.
Worker is not currently connected to the horde and cannot process jobs.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_low_spee: Worker is performing below expected speed thresholds and is considered a 'slow_worker'. Users can spend additional kudos using the `slow_workers: false` option to skip these workers and get faster results.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_high_spe: Worker is performing above usual speed thresholds. This can be normal for high-end GPUs or certain models, but may also indicate inaccurate reporting or other anomalies.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_paused.d: Worker has been paused by the system due for suspicious activity. Only moderators can see this.
help.glossary.page.workers.icon_maintena: Worker is in maintenance mode, it will finish current jobs but not accept new ones.
Worker has been flagged by moderators for policy violations or suspicious behavior.
Worker belongs to a trusted user. Most users become trusted after about a week of consistent activity.
help.glossary.page.workers.badge_img2img: Worker supports image-to-image generation, transforming an input image based on a prompt.
help.glossary.page.workers.badge_inpaint: Worker supports inpainting/outpainting, selectively regenerating masked areas of an image.
help.glossary.page.workers.badge_post_pr: Worker supports post-processing operations such as upscaling and face-fixing.
help.glossary.page.workers.badge_lora.de: Worker supports LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) models for fine-tuned style and subject generation.
help.glossary.page.workers.badge_control: Worker supports ControlNet for guided image generation using structural inputs like depth maps or edge detection.
help.glossary.terms.ai_horde.title: AI Horde
help.glossary.terms.ai_horde.body: A volunteer-powered distributed cluster for AI image and text generation. Instead of relying on a central server, the processing power comes from volunteers who share their GPUs.
help.glossary.terms.kudos.title: Kudos
help.glossary.terms.kudos.body: The priority system of the AI Horde. Workers earn kudos for processing jobs, and users spend kudos for higher priority in the queue. Kudos never expire and cannot be sold (but they can be gifted to other users); they represent your contribution to the community.
help.glossary.terms.request.title: Request
help.glossary.terms.request.body: One press of Generate: the prompt and settings you sent, and the images asked for with them. Asking for four images is still one request, and each image is a separate job for a worker.
help.glossary.terms.request.body_images: The number of images requested over the life of the account. This can be higher than the number of requests made if some requests included multiple images (e.g. requesting 4 images counts as 1 request but 4 jobs).
help.glossary.terms.request.body_text: The number of text generations requested over the life of the account. This can be higher than the number of requests made if some requests included multiple generations (e.g. requesting 3 responses counts as 1 request but 3 jobs).
help.glossary.terms.job.title: Job
help.glossary.terms.job.body: A single unit of work derived from a request. For example, a request for 4 images becomes 4 jobs, each producing one image. Jobs are distributed to available workers.
help.glossary.terms.model.title: Model
help.glossary.terms.model.body: A trained AI file that a worker loads to perform generation. Different models produce different styles and quality; for example, Stable Diffusion for images or LLaMA for text. Workers choose which models to load.
help.glossary.terms.team.title: Team
help.glossary.terms.team.body: A group of workers organized by their owners. Teams can pool contributions and appear on the leaderboard. Joining a team is optional.
help.glossary.terms.trusted.title: Trusted
help.glossary.terms.trusted.body: A user status earned by running a worker reliably for at least one week. Trusted users get additional privileges and their workers receive priority.
help.glossary.terms.nsfw.title: NSFW Filter
help.glossary.terms.nsfw.body: Controls whether a worker accepts Not Safe For Work requests. Workers with NSFW disabled will skip such jobs. This is set by each worker's operator.
help.glossary.terms.worker.title: Worker
help.glossary.terms.worker.body: A volunteer's computer (typically with a GPU) running bridge software to process AI generation requests. Workers earn kudos for their owners.
help.glossary.terms.dreamer.title: Dreamer (Image Worker)
help.glossary.terms.dreamer.body: A worker that generates images from text prompts (text-to-image) or from other images (image-to-image). Uses models like Stable Diffusion.
help.glossary.terms.scribe.title: Scribe (Text Worker)
help.glossary.terms.scribe.body: A worker that generates text responses using large language models (LLMs). Typically requires GPUs with large amounts of VRAM.
help.glossary.terms.alchemist.title: Alchemist (Alchemy Worker)
help.glossary.terms.alchemist.body: A worker that performs image utility operations: captioning (describing images), interrogation (analyzing image content), and upscaling. Some of these operations run on an ordinary CPU, so an alchemist can contribute even without a graphics card.
help.glossary.terms.bridge_agent.title: Bridge Agent
help.glossary.terms.bridge_agent.body: The software that connects a volunteer's GPU to the AI Horde network. It polls for jobs, runs the AI model locally, and returns results. Examples include AI Horde Worker and hordelib.
help.glossary.terms.text2img.title: Text-to-Image (txt2img)
help.glossary.terms.text2img.body: The standard generation mode: a text description (prompt) is converted into an image by the AI model through a diffusion process.
help.glossary.terms.img2img.title: Image-to-Image (img2img)
help.glossary.terms.img2img.body: A generation mode that uses an existing image as a starting point, then modifies it according to a text prompt. Useful for style transfer and guided editing.
help.glossary.terms.inpainting.title: Inpainting
help.glossary.terms.inpainting.body: Selectively regenerating a masked region of an image while keeping the surrounding area intact. Used for removing, adding, or changing specific parts of an image.
help.glossary.terms.outpainting.title: Outpainting
help.glossary.terms.outpainting.body: Growing a picture past its original edges and having the model fill in the new space. The horde treats it as inpainting with the added border as the masked area, so the tool you are using has to place your picture in the larger canvas itself.
help.glossary.terms.steps.title: Steps
help.glossary.terms.steps.body: How many denoising passes a model makes on its way from noise to a picture. More steps cost more time and more kudos, and most models stop improving somewhere between 20 and 40.
help.glossary.terms.cfg.title: Guidance (CFG scale)
help.glossary.terms.cfg.body: How strictly the model is pushed to follow your prompt. Low values let it wander and invent; high values force every word in and tend to look over-baked.
help.glossary.terms.sampler.title: Sampler
help.glossary.terms.sampler.body: The algorithm that turns the starting noise into an image. Samplers differ in character and in how quickly they settle rather than in quality.
help.glossary.terms.seed.title: Seed
help.glossary.terms.seed.body: The number an image's starting noise is generated from. The same seed with the same settings and model gives the same image every time.
help.glossary.terms.clip_skip.title: CLIP skip
help.glossary.terms.clip_skip.body: Stops reading your prompt a number of layers before the end of the text encoder, which hands the model a looser reading of it. 1 is standard; many anime-derived checkpoints were trained at 2.
help.glossary.terms.karras.title: Karras schedule
help.glossary.terms.karras.body: A way of spacing the noise levels a sampler works through, spending more of the steps at the low-noise end. It often sharpens the result at low step counts.
help.glossary.terms.hires_fix.title: Hires fix
help.glossary.terms.hires_fix.body: Renders at the model's native size first, then upscales that image and repaints it. It avoids the duplicated limbs a model produces when asked for a picture much larger than it was trained on.
help.glossary.terms.denoise.title: Denoising strength
help.glossary.terms.denoise.body: How much of a source image the model is allowed to repaint. Low values leave your picture with a light pass over it; near 1 almost nothing of the original survives.
help.glossary.terms.tiling.title: Tiling
help.glossary.terms.tiling.body: Makes the edges of an image wrap, so copies laid side by side join without a seam. Worth having for backgrounds and textures meant to repeat.
help.glossary.terms.lora.title: LoRA
help.glossary.terms.lora.body: Low-Rank Adaptation: a lightweight model add-on that modifies generation style without replacing the base model. LoRAs are small files that can add specific characters, styles, or concepts.
help.glossary.terms.controlnet.title: ControlNet
help.glossary.terms.controlnet.body: An advanced technique that uses reference images (like edge maps, depth maps, or pose skeletons) to precisely control the composition and structure of generated images.
help.glossary.terms.post_processing.body: Enhancements applied after image generation, such as upscaling (increasing resolution), face fixing (GFPGAN/CodeFormers), and other quality improvements.
help.glossary.terms.maintenance.title: Maintenance Mode
help.glossary.terms.maintenance.body: A worker state set by its owner indicating it's temporarily offline. The worker won't accept new jobs until maintenance mode is cleared.
help.glossary.terms.paused.title: Paused
help.glossary.terms.paused.body: A worker state set by moderators. A paused worker cannot accept jobs until a moderator unpauses it. This is typically used for investigation.
help.glossary.terms.flagged.title: Flagged
help.glossary.terms.flagged.body: A worker that has been flagged by moderators for investigation, typically due to suspicious output, slow performance, or rule violations.
help.glossary.terms.threads.title: Threads
help.glossary.terms.threads.body: The number of jobs a worker can process simultaneously. More threads increase throughput but require more GPU memory and compute power.
help.glossary.terms.megapixelsteps.title: Megapixelsteps (MPS)
help.glossary.terms.megapixelsteps.body: A unit measuring image generation work: megapixels × diffusion steps. One megapixel is a 1024×1024 image. A 20-step generation of a 1024×1024 image equals 20 megapixelsteps.
help.glossary.terms.tokens.title: Tokens
help.glossary.terms.tokens.body: The basic unit of text for language models. One token is roughly 0.75 words (or about 4 characters). Text generation speed is measured in tokens per second.
help.glossary.terms.eta.title: ETA (Estimated Time)
help.glossary.terms.eta.body: The estimated time until a model's queue is cleared, calculated from current queue depth divided by current processing speed.
help.glossary.terms.uptime.title: Uptime
help.glossary.terms.uptime.body: How long a worker has been continuously connected and processing jobs since it last started.
help.glossary.terms.api_key.title: API Key
help.glossary.terms.api_key.body: A secret key that identifies you to the AI Horde. You can use the anonymous key (0000000000) to try the service immediately, or register for a personal key to earn kudos and get higher priority.
help.glossary.terms.queue.title: Queue
help.glossary.terms.queue.body: When you submit a generation request, it enters a queue. Workers pick up jobs from the queue in priority order; users with more kudos are served first. Queue depth indicates how much work is waiting.
help.glossary.terms.gui.title: GUI (Frontend)
help.glossary.terms.gui.body: A graphical user interface that lets you use the AI Horde without writing code. Frontends provide visual tools for creating images or text with features like prompt editors, image galleries, and parameter controls.
help.glossary.terms.sdk.title: SDK / Library
help.glossary.terms.sdk.body: A software development kit or code library that lets programmers integrate AI Horde into their own applications. Available in various programming languages.
help.glossary.terms.cli.title: CLI Tool
help.glossary.terms.cli.body: A command-line interface tool: software you run from a terminal or command prompt rather than a graphical window. Useful for scripting and automation.
help.glossary.terms.bot.title: Bot
help.glossary.terms.bot.body: An automated program that connects AI Horde to a chat platform like Discord or Telegram, letting users generate images or text through chat commands.
help.glossary.terms.utility.title: Utility
help.glossary.terms.utility.body: A helper tool that works alongside the AI Horde, such as model browsers, prompt generators, or workflow managers. Not a full frontend, but adds useful functionality.
help.styles.title: What are Styles?
help.styles.subtitle: Reusable generation presets shared by the community
help.styles.body:
Styles are saved generation presets (a combination of prompt template, model, and parameters) that anyone can create and share. Using a style lets you reproduce a specific look or technique without manually configuring every setting.

Image styles include settings like the model, sampler, CFG scale, steps, and LoRAs. Text styles include parameters like temperature, top-p, and stop sequences. Styles can be public (visible to everyone) or private (only visible to the creator).

Browse styles by category, search by name or tag, and click any style to see its full configuration and example outputs.
help.teams.title: What are Teams?
help.teams.subtitle: Groups of workers organized by their owners
help.teams.body:
Teams let worker operators organize their volunteer GPUs into named groups. A team pools the contributions of its member workers, making it easy to track collective impact.

Each team shows its total workers, accumulated kudos (priority credits earned by processing jobs), and requests fulfilled. Teams appear on the leaderboard and provide a way for organizations or groups of friends to contribute together.

Any trusted user can create a team and assign their workers to it. Workers can only belong to one team at a time.
help.leaderboard.title: What is the Kudos Leaderboard?
help.leaderboard.subtitle: Ranking the most generous contributors to the network
help.leaderboard.body:
The Kudos Leaderboard ranks AI Horde users by their unspent kudos balance. High balances represent people who have contributed far more computing power (by running workers) than they have consumed; they are the backbone of the volunteer network.

Kudos are priority credits: workers earn them by processing generation jobs, and users spend them for faster queue times. Kudos never expire and cannot be sold for money, but they can be gifted to other users. A large balance simply means someone has been very generous with their GPU time.

You can find your own rank using the "Find Your Rank" feature if you're logged in.
help.users.title: User Lookup
help.users.subtitle: Find and view any AI Horde user's public profile
help.users.body:
Look up any AI Horde user by their numeric ID or full username (e.g., 'alias#123') to see their public profile information.

User profiles show kudos balance, worker count, account age, and contribution statistics. You can also navigate to their workers and teams from the profile page.

The Kudos Leaderboard is another way to browse top contributors.
help.profile_guest.title: Your AI Horde Profile
help.profile_guest.subtitle: View your kudos, workers, teams, and generation history
help.profile_guest.body:
Your profile shows your kudos balance (priority credits), generation history, worker statistics, and team memberships. You can also manage shared API keys and custom styles from here.

To view your profile, enter your API key, the account key you received when you registered. Your key is only used to fetch your data and is stored locally in your browser.

Don't have an account? Register for free to get an API key, earn kudos, and track your contributions. You can use AI Horde anonymously, but registered users earn kudos for higher priority.

mission_callout.title: Our Mission
mission_callout.description: AI Horde is a free, community-powered service that provides open access to generative AI. We are a volunteer-run, non-profit effort dedicated to ensuring powerful machine learning technologies remain available to all people, regardless of their financial means or technical resources.
mission.title: Our Mission
mission.subtitle: AI Horde exists because we believe transformative technology should belong to everyone, not just those who can afford it.
mission.statement.title: Mission Statement
mission.statement.body: AI Horde is a free, community-powered service that provides open access to generative AI. We are a volunteer-run, non-profit effort dedicated to ensuring that powerful machine learning technologies remain available to all people, regardless of their financial means, geographic location, or technical resources. We believe that when people freely share what they have, everyone gains more than any one person gives up.
mission.why.title: Why We Exist
mission.why.paragraph1: Generative AI is among the most transformative technologies of our time. It is reshaping how people create art, write, learn, conduct research, and solve problems. But running these models demands expensive hardware: powerful GPUs that most people simply cannot afford. Left to market forces alone, access to these capabilities concentrates in the hands of well-funded corporations and the individuals wealthy enough to pay for subscriptions.
mission.why.paragraph2: We reject the premise that your economic circumstances should determine whether you can use these tools. A student in Lagos deserves the same access to AI-assisted learning as a developer in San Francisco. An independent artist should not be priced out of creative tools that could transform their work. A researcher at an underfunded university should not have to choose between their budget and their curiosity.
mission.why.paragraph3: AI Horde was built to break that pattern. In the tradition of volunteer computing projects like Folding@home and SETI@home, we connect people who have spare computing power with people who need it. The result is a distributed cluster that belongs to no single entity, a shared resource sustained by collective generosity.
mission.values.title: What We Stand For
mission.values.access.title: Universal Access, No Exceptions
mission.values.access.description: Everyone can use AI Horde for free, even anonymously. No credit card, no paywall, and no way to buy priority. AI Horde is a registered non-profit, and our kudos system is designed so that priority can only be earned by contributing compute, not purchased. Access to transformative technology is not a privilege.
mission.values.solidarity.title: Mutual Aid
mission.values.solidarity.description: Our entire model depends on people choosing to help strangers. Volunteers donate their idle compute so that others can create, learn, and build. Most earned kudos go unspent: a quiet, ongoing act of generosity.
mission.values.openness.title: Open Source, Open Knowledge
mission.values.openness.description: We exclusively use and promote open-source models and software. Machine learning was built on decades of shared research, and we believe it should stay open. Education, art, science, and the public good all depend on it.
mission.track_record.title: The Record So Far
mission.track_record.intro: These are not aspirations. AI Horde has been doing this, continuously, since 2022.
mission.track_record.scale.paragraph1: AI Horde has generated over 170 million images and fulfilled more than 250 million text requests, entirely through volunteer-donated compute. On any given day, tens of thousands of images and hundreds of thousands of text completions pass through a distributed network of volunteer GPUs around the world.
mission.track_record.engineering.paragra: The Haidra organisation maintains over 30 open-source repositories covering the core service, worker software, model catalogues, developer tools, and more. Over 300 releases have been shipped through the efforts of 100+ contributors. Everything is publicly available, auditable, and designed to be extended by anyone.
mission.track_record.community.paragraph: The real measure of decentralisation is not the software we maintain - it is the ecosystem built around it. Dozens of independent front ends, GUIs, bots, and integrations have been created by developers outside the core team. The Haidra team are stewards of the centralised infrastructure. The community that has grown around it is the real story.
mission.crowdsourcing.title: The Power of Crowdsourcing
mission.crowdsourcing.paragraph1: Crowdsourcing only works when people are willing to give without guaranteed return. Every volunteer who runs a worker is choosing to spend their own electricity, wear on their own hardware, and dedicate their own time, not for payment, but because they believe others should have access to these tools too.
mission.crowdsourcing.paragraph2: This is not a business model. It is an act of solidarity. The volunteers who power AI Horde come from all over the world, united by a shared conviction that technology should serve people, not extract from them. Some run workers around the clock. Others contribute during off-hours when their machines would otherwise sit idle. All of them make the service possible.
mission.crowdsourcing.paragraph3: The kudos system ensures fairness without introducing money. Workers earn kudos by fulfilling requests, and those kudos grant priority for their own future requests. But kudos can never be bought or sold. They represent contributed effort, and nothing else. Those who leave their kudos unspent are effectively donating their compute to anonymous users and newcomers who have none, ensuring the system remains open even to people who have nothing to give back yet.
mission.free_access.title: Why Free Access Matters
mission.free_access.paragraph1: Commercial AI services impose subscriptions, usage caps, and terms that can change without notice. They decide what you can generate, what models you can use, and what happens to your data. When access depends on payment, entire populations are excluded: those in developing nations, students, hobbyists, independent researchers, and anyone living under economic hardship.
mission.free_access.paragraph2: Free access is not just a convenience. It is a statement about who gets to participate in the future. Generative AI is a general-purpose tool with applications across art, education, accessibility, science, and personal expression. Allowing that access to be gated by ability to pay means accepting that these benefits are only for the privileged.
mission.free_access.paragraph3: AI Horde ensures that a baseline of access always exists: one that no corporation can revoke, no terms change can eliminate, and no price increase can put out of reach. As long as volunteers are willing to share, the service endures.
mission.hedge.title: What We Guard Against
mission.hedge.paragraph1: The centralization of AI behind corporate paywalls poses a real threat to the open ecosystem that made these technologies possible in the first place. Large language models and image generators were built on openly published research, publicly available datasets, and community-driven development. When the resulting tools are locked behind subscription fees, the public effectively pays twice: once through the shared knowledge that trained the models, and again for the privilege of using them.
mission.hedge.paragraph2: We also guard against the erosion of choice. When a handful of providers control access to generative AI, they also control what content can be created, which use cases are permitted, and whose values are encoded into the system. A decentralized, volunteer-driven alternative ensures that no single entity holds that power.
mission.hedge.paragraph3: AI Horde is not opposed to commercial AI services existing. But we believe a non-commercial alternative must also exist: one that is accountable to its community rather than to shareholders, and one that prioritizes public benefit over revenue.
mission.commitments.title: Our Commitments
mission.commitments.nonprofit.title: Non-Profit, Now and Always
mission.commitments.nonprofit.descriptio: Haidra, the organization behind AI Horde, is a registered non-profit association (ASBL) under Luxembourg law. No surplus is ever distributed to members or third parties. All funds go directly toward sustaining and improving the service for the public.
mission.commitments.opensource.title: Open Source First
mission.commitments.opensource.descripti: All AI Horde software is open source. We use and promote open-source models exclusively. Closed-source models do not align with our vision of democratized access. Transparency is not optional. It is foundational.
mission.commitments.nocommodification.de: Kudos cannot be bought or sold. Priority is earned through contribution, not payment. We will never introduce a paid tier, a premium queue, or any mechanism that lets money buy faster access. The service is free, and that is a promise.
mission.commitments.community.title: Community Governance
mission.commitments.community.descriptio: AI Horde is shaped by its community. Decisions about the service are made transparently, with input from the volunteers, developers, and users who sustain it. The people who build and power the system have a voice in how it evolves.
mission.haidra.title: About Haidra
mission.haidra.paragraph1: Haidra is the volunteer organization behind AI Horde. Registered as a non-profit association in Luxembourg, Haidra's objectives include increasing access to free and open-source machine learning technologies, supporting education, facilitating open development, and promoting the free flow of information. Our articles of association explicitly state that the Association's actions shall never unfairly benefit private interests over public ones.
mission.haidra.paragraph2: The name reflects what we are: a collective of developers, operators, advocates, and users working together because we believe these tools should exist in the commons. We are not a company. We have no investors, no revenue targets, and no exit strategy. We are here because this work matters.
mission.cta.title: Join Us
mission.cta.description: AI Horde is made possible by people who believe technology should serve everyone. Whether you have a spare GPU, a few dollars, or simply want to use what the community has built, you are welcome here.
